fields.title: Exodus
fields.subtitle: Shemot, “Names”
fields.description: The second book of the Bible, called in Hebrew Shemot from its opening words, “These are the names”, and in Greek Exodus, “the way out”. A new king who had never heard of Joseph turns Jacob’s family into slaves, and God hears their groaning and remembers his covenant. Then the great story of rescue: the baby hidden among the reeds of the Nile, the bush that burns and does not burn away, the name “I AM WHO I AM”, the plagues, the Passover lamb, and the sea split open. In the wilderness come manna and water from the rock; at Sinai, the Ten Commandments and the covenant sealed in blood; and after the golden calf, Moses’ prayer, the LORD passing by and proclaiming his name, and the glory filling the tabernacle. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Hebrew given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the book’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the book of Exodus?
qa.answer: The second book of the Bible and of the five books of Moses, the Torah. Its Hebrew name, Shemot, “Names”, comes from its opening words; the name Exodus, Greek for “going out”, comes from the ancient Greek translation. Its forty chapters tell how God rescued Jacob’s descendants from slavery in Egypt (chapters 1–15), led them through the wilderness (15–18), and at Mount Sinai made a covenant with them, gave them his law and came to live among them in the tabernacle (19–40).

qa.question: Who wrote the book of Exodus, and when did the exodus happen?
qa.answer: Exodus does not name its author, though it says that Moses wrote down some of its words (17:14; 24:4; 34:27), and Jewish and Christian tradition has received it as one of the five books of Moses. Many scholars think it drew on older sources and reached its final form much later. The date of the exodus is also debated: some place it in the fifteenth century BC, from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1; many place it in the thirteenth, from the city of Rameses named in Exodus 1:11. Christians hold a range of views on both questions.

qa.question: What are the Ten Commandments?
qa.answer: The words God spoke from Mount Sinai in Exodus 20:1–17, repeated in Deuteronomy 5; the Hebrew calls them “the Ten Words” (34:28). They begin not with a command but with a reminder of rescue: “I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house where you were slaves.” Then come no other gods, no idols, no misuse of God’s name, the Sabbath, honour to parents, and no murder, adultery, theft, false evidence or coveting. Jewish, Catholic and Lutheran, and Orthodox and Reformed traditions divide the same words into ten in slightly different ways.

qa.question: What does “I AM WHO I AM” mean in Exodus 3:14?
qa.answer: It is God’s answer when Moses asks his name at the burning bush. The words come from the Hebrew verb “to be”, and God’s personal name, written in English Bibles as “the LORD”, is closely related to them. They have been understood as a promise of faithful presence (“I will be who I will be”, echoing “I will be with you” in 3:12), as a statement of God’s freedom, and as a declaration that God simply is, depending on nothing. In John 8:58 Jesus says, “before Abraham was, I am”, and many readers hear this name behind it.

qa.question: Why does Exodus spend so many chapters on the tabernacle?
qa.answer: Because the tabernacle is the goal of the rescue. God tells Moses, “They are to make me a sanctuary, so that I may dwell among them” (25:8), and says he brought Israel out of Egypt “to make my home among them” (29:46). The plans are given in chapters 25–31 and the building is described in chapters 35–40, with the golden calf in between, and the book ends with the glory of the LORD filling the tent. The New Testament takes up the picture: John says the Word “made his home among us”, and the letter to the Hebrews reads the tabernacle as a copy and shadow of the heavenly sanctuary that Christ has entered.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” And he said, “Tell the Israelites this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

— Exodus 3:14

Exodus is the Bible’s great story of rescue. In Hebrew it is called Shemot, “Names”, from its opening words, “These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob.” The name we use comes from the ancient Greek translation and means “going out”, or “the way out”. Both names are fitting. The book begins with a list of names, a family of seventy people, and it ends with a nation camped around the dwelling place of God. In between is the way out.

It picks up exactly where Genesis left off. Joseph has died in Egypt, asking to be carried home when God comes to help his people. Exodus tells how God came. But it tells much more than an escape. The people who are led out of slavery are led to a mountain, where God binds himself to them by covenant, and then he does something stranger still: he tells them to build him a tent, so that he can live among them on the road.

That is the shape of the whole book. God hears, God rescues, God speaks, and God comes to stay.

Three places

Exodus is easiest to follow by where it happens. Chapters 1–15 are set in Egypt and at its border: the slavery, the call of Moses, the plagues, the Passover night and the crossing of the sea. Chapters 15–18 are a journey through the wilderness, with hunger, thirst, battle and a father-in-law’s good advice. And chapters 19–40 take place at the foot of Mount Sinai, where the people stay for the rest of the book.

The proportions are surprising. More than half the book is spent at Sinai, on laws and on the plans for the tabernacle, the portable sanctuary, given in chapters 25–31 and carried out almost word for word in chapters 35–40. Between the plan and the building comes the worst moment in the book, the golden calf. Exodus thinks that what God does with a rescued people matters as much as the rescue itself.

A king who had never heard of Joseph

The book opens with a blessing coming true. The Israelites “were fruitful; they teemed and multiplied”, echoing God’s blessing at creation. Then a new king comes to the throne, “one who had never heard of Joseph”, and sees in that growth only a threat. He enslaves them, and when that does not work, he orders every Hebrew boy thrown into the Nile.

The first people in Exodus to resist him are two midwives, Shiphrah and Puah. They are named; the Pharaoh is not. “But the midwives feared God”, and they kept the boys alive. Then comes a chain of women who outwit the most powerful man in the world: a mother who hides her son, a sister who watches from the reeds, and Pharaoh’s own daughter, who takes pity on a crying Hebrew baby and raises him in the palace. She names him Moses, “because,” she says, “I pulled him out of the water.”

Moses grows up, kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew, and has to flee. He spends years as a shepherd in Midian. And then the narrator turns back to Egypt with a few short sentences that change everything:

God heard how they groaned, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God looked upon the Israelites, and God took notice.

— Exodus 2:24–25

The bush and the name

At Horeb, the mountain of God, Moses sees a bush on fire that does not burn away, and turns aside to look. God calls him by name, tells him to take off his sandals because “the place where you stand is holy ground”, and says that he has seen the misery of his people: “I have come down to rescue them.”

Moses objects, again and again. “Who am I to go to Pharaoh, and to bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” God answers not by telling Moses who he is but by promising who will go with him: “I will be with you.” Then Moses asks what he should say when the people ask God’s name, and God answers with the sentence at the head of this introduction, “I AM WHO I AM.” The words come from the Hebrew verb “to be”, and the personal name of God, written in this translation as “the LORD”, is closely related to them. They have been read in more than one way: as God’s faithful presence (“I will be who I will be”), as his freedom from anyone’s control, and as his being itself, the one who simply is. They may mean all of these. God goes on: “That is my name for all time.”

Moses has more excuses, until he says plainly, “Please, Lord, send someone else.” God is angry, but he gives him his brother Aaron to speak for him, and sends him back.

“Release my people”

Pharaoh’s first answer sets the terms of everything that follows: “Who is the LORD, that I should do what he says and release Israel? I do not know the LORD.” The plagues are God’s reply. Water turns to blood; frogs, gnats, flies, disease, boils, hail, locusts and darkness fall on Egypt, until the tenth and last. Again and again the purpose is stated: “the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.” The Nile, the land, the sun: the powers Egypt worshiped are shown to be creatures, and against “all the gods of Egypt” the LORD carries out judgment.

Readers have always noticed that Pharaoh’s stubbornness is described in two ways. Sometimes Pharaoh hardens his own heart; sometimes the LORD hardens it; sometimes it simply stays stubborn. Christians have weighed these sentences differently, some stressing God’s sovereign purpose (Paul quotes 9:16 in Romans 9:17), others that God confirmed a choice Pharaoh had already made. The text holds both together and does not let either Pharaoh or the reader off the hook.

The Passover

Before the last plague God gives Israel a meal. Each household is to kill a lamb, “a sound, unblemished male in its first year”, put its blood on the doorposts, and eat it in haste, dressed for the road, “robes tucked into your belts, sandals on, staffs in hand.”

The blood will mark the houses where you are staying; it will be a sign for you. I will see the blood and pass over you, and the plague that destroys will not fall on you when I strike the land of Egypt.

— Exodus 12:13

Notice that the meal is designed to be repeated, and to be explained. “In time your children will say to you, ‘What is this service of yours about?’” The story of the exodus is meant to be told at the table, by parents to children, in every generation. And notice that the deliverance comes through blood and through a substitute: the firstborn of Israel live because a lamb has died. The apostle Paul could write, with no further explanation, “For Christ has been sacrificed as our Passover lamb.” Jesus himself chose the Passover meal to give his disciples the bread and the cup.

Through the sea

Pharaoh lets the people go, then changes his mind, and the Israelites find themselves trapped between the sea and the chariots of Egypt. They panic, and turn on Moses with a bitter joke: “Did Egypt have no graves, that you had to bring us out here to die in the wilderness?” His answer is one of the great sentences of faith:

But Moses told the people, “Have no fear! Hold your ground and watch how the LORD will save you today. You see the Egyptians today, but you will never see them again. The LORD will fight on your behalf, and you can stay quiet.”

— Exodus 14:13–14

The sea opens, the people walk through “on dry ground”, and the waters come back over the army that follows. Chapter 15 answers the deliverance with a song, the first long song in the Bible: “My strength and my song is the LORD; he has come to save me.” Miriam takes up a tambourine and leads the women in its refrain. At its heart is a question that the rest of Scripture keeps asking:

Among the gods, who compares with you, O LORD? Who is like you, splendid in holiness, fearsome in deeds of praise, doer of wonders?

— Exodus 15:11

Bread from heaven

Three days later they are grumbling. The water at Marah is bitter; the food has run out; they look back on Egypt, of all places, with longing: “There we sat beside the pots of meat.” The wilderness chapters are honest about how quickly rescued people forget. They are just as honest about how patient God is. He makes the bitter water sweet. He rains down bread from heaven, a strange flaky food the people call manna, from their own question, “What is it?” Each day there is enough for that day, and on the sixth day enough for the Sabbath as well.

At Rephidim there is no water, and the people quarrel with Moses and put the LORD to the test by asking, “Is the LORD among us or not?” Moses strikes the rock at Horeb, and water pours out. Then the Amalekites attack, and Israel prevails only while Moses holds up his hands, until Aaron and Hur sit him on a stone and hold them up for him “until the sun set.” Even Moses cannot do it alone, as Jethro tells him in chapter 18: “The load is too heavy for you; you cannot carry it by yourself.”

Eagles’ wings: the covenant at Sinai

In the third month the people reach Sinai, and God speaks to them from the mountain. Before he gives them a single command, he reminds them what he has already done: “how I lifted you up on eagles’ wings and brought you here to me.” Only then does he offer them a covenant, to be his “own special treasure”, “a kingdom of priests and a holy nation”. The order matters. The law is not the way Israel earns God’s rescue. It is the shape of life for people who have already been rescued.

The Ten Commandments themselves begin the same way: “I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house where you were slaves.” Then come the words that Jews and Christians have learned by heart: no other gods, no idols, no misuse of the name, the Sabbath day, honour to parents, and no murder, adultery, theft, false evidence or coveting. The first commands are about God, the rest about the neighbour, and Jesus would later sum up the whole law in love for both.

Chapters 21–23, often called the Book of the Covenant, apply those commands to the life of a farming people: slaves and their release, injuries, property, loans and justice in court. Some of these laws are hard for modern readers, and they come from a world very unlike ours. But again and again they turn to the weak, with a reason drawn from Israel’s own story:

Do not oppress a foreigner living among you. You know from the inside what a foreigner’s life is like, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

— Exodus 23:9

Then the covenant is sealed. Moses reads the scroll to the people, and they answer, “We will listen and obey.” He dashes blood on the altar and on the people:

Moses took the blood and dashed it over the people. “Look,” he said, “the blood of the covenant, which the LORD has made with you on the terms of all these words.”

— Exodus 24:8

And the elders go up the mountain, and see the God of Israel, “and they ate and drank.” Centuries later, at another meal, Jesus took a cup and said, “This is my blood of the covenant, poured out for many.”

A tent for God

Moses goes up into the cloud for forty days, and what God gives him there is not more law but a building plan:

They are to make me a sanctuary, so that I may dwell among them.

— Exodus 25:8

Readers often stall in these chapters, with their curtains, acacia wood and gold. But they are among the most moving in the book, once you see what they are for. The God who thundered on the mountain means to travel with his people in a tent. At its centre is the ark, and over the ark the mercy seat, where God says, “I will meet with you there.” The priests’ garments, the lampstand, the altar of incense: everything is made to “the pattern” God shows Moses, as though the tent were a copy of something greater. And the reason is given plainly: “I brought them out of the land of Egypt for this purpose, to make my home among them.” The goal of the exodus was not only freedom from Pharaoh. It was life with God.

The golden calf

While God is giving Moses the plans for his dwelling, the people at the foot of the mountain are making a god of their own. Moses has been gone too long; they want gods “to lead the way for us”. Aaron collects their gold and makes a calf, and they cry, “Israel, these are your gods, who brought you up from the land of Egypt!” The covenant is broken within weeks of being made, and Moses, coming down the mountain, smashes the tablets.

What follows is one of the great passages on prayer in the Bible. God tells Moses to let him alone, that he may destroy the people and make a new nation from Moses. Moses will not let him alone. He pleads God’s reputation among the Egyptians and God’s promises to Abraham, Isaac and Israel, and “the LORD relented from the harm he had said he would do to his people.” He even offers himself: if God will not forgive them, “then blot me out of your book that you have written.”

The crisis is now about presence. God offers to send an angel ahead of them, but not to go himself. Moses answers, “Unless your presence goes with us, do not make us leave this place.” In the tent outside the camp, the LORD speaks with him “face to face, the way a person talks with a friend.” And Moses asks for the boldest thing of all: “Please, let me see your glory.” God hides him in a cleft of the rock, covers him with his hand, and passes by, proclaiming his own name:

The LORD passed in front of Moses and called out, “The LORD, the LORD, a God of tender compassion and grace, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love and in truth, who keeps faithful love for thousands and forgives wrongdoing, rebellion and sin. Yet he will never acquit the guilty; he brings the wrongdoing of parents upon their children and grandchildren, to the third and the fourth generation.”

— Exodus 34:6–7

Few passages are echoed more often within the Old Testament itself. It echoes through the Psalms and the prophets, from Joel to Jonah. It is God’s own account of his character, given at the moment his people least deserved it, and it holds mercy and justice together without letting go of either.

Glory fills the tent

The covenant is renewed, and Moses comes down with his face shining, so that he has to cover it with a veil. Then the people bring their gifts, more than enough, and the tabernacle is built exactly as God commanded. The last scene of the book is the answer to everything that went before:

Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the tabernacle was filled with the glory of the LORD.

— Exodus 40:34

The book that began with God hearing the groans of slaves ends with God living in their camp, “at every stage of their travels.”

How to read Exodus

Read the story chapters, 1–20 and 32–34, at a good pace; they are some of the most gripping narrative in Scripture. Take the laws of chapters 21–23 slowly and ask what each one protects. In the tabernacle chapters, keep asking the question they answer: how can a holy God live among a sinful people? Leviticus, the next book, takes up that question at length.

Exodus does not name its author. It says that Moses wrote down some of its words (17:14; 24:4; 34:27), and Jewish and Christian tradition has received it as the second of the five books of Moses. Many scholars think it was drawn together from older sources and reached its final form much later. There is also debate about when the exodus happened: some date it to the fifteenth century BC, from the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1; others to the thirteenth, from the city of Rameses named in 1:11. Christians hold a range of views on these questions, while agreeing that the God who acts in this book is the God who raised Jesus from the dead.

Watch for the echoes. Moses is drawn out of the water in an “ark”, the same word as Noah’s. The plagues undo creation, and the sea is split as the waters were divided in Genesis 1. Israel is called God’s firstborn son (4:22), and the firstborn of Egypt die. The people complain in the wilderness, and Moses prays for them. And notice how often the book tells you that something is to be remembered, retold, explained to children. Exodus means to become your story too.

About this translation

The text in this edition is the Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Hebrew and given freely to the public domain. It is printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. A few of its choices in Exodus are worth knowing before you begin.

“The LORD.” Exodus is the book in which God tells Moses his personal name, the four Hebrew letters often written Yahweh. Following long Jewish and Christian custom, this translation prints it as “the LORD” in capitals. At the burning bush it keeps the familiar “I AM WHO I AM” for God’s explanation of the name.

“Faithful love.” The Hebrew word hesed, older Bibles’ “mercy” or “steadfast love”, is the love that keeps covenant. Here it is “faithful love”: God shows it “to thousands who love me and keep my commandments”, and is “rich in faithful love and in truth.”

“The Ten Words.” What we call the Ten Commandments the Hebrew calls “the Ten Words”, and the translation keeps that name where it occurs (34:28).

Measures and names. Ancient measures are given in modern terms, so a day’s manna is “about 2 quarts” for every person. The sea Israel crossed keeps its long-familiar name, the Red Sea.

For the reasoning behind every sentence of the translation, with the Hebrew beside it, see the Open Word Bible itself at openwordbible.org.

fields.title: Exodus 1
fields.body_html:
Israel grows in Egypt

These are the names of the sons of Israel who came to Egypt with Jacob, each one bringing his household: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, and Judah, Issachar, Zebulun, and Benjamin, Dan and Naphtali, Gad and Asher. Seventy people in all were descended from Jacob. Joseph himself was already in Egypt. In time Joseph died, and so did all his brothers and everyone of that generation. But the Israelites were fruitful; they teemed and multiplied and grew exceedingly strong, until the land was full of them.

A new king oppresses Israel

Then a new king came to the throne of Egypt, one who had never heard of Joseph. He said to his people, “See how the people of the Israelites have become too many and too strong for us. Come, we must outwit them, or they will grow even more numerous. Then, if there is a war, they could side with our enemies, fight us, and escape from the land.” So the Egyptians put taskmasters over them to crush them with heavy loads, and the Israelites built supply cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Rameses. Yet the harder they were oppressed, the more they increased and spread out, until the Egyptians came to loathe and fear the Israelites. The Egyptians forced the Israelites to work without mercy, and made their lives bitter with hard labor, mixing mortar, making bricks, and doing every kind of work in the fields. In all this labor they drove them without mercy. The king of Egypt also spoke to the Hebrew midwives, one named Shiphrah and the other Puah. He said, “When you attend the Hebrew women in childbirth, watch as they kneel on the birthstones. If it is a son, put him to death; if a daughter, she may live.” But the midwives feared God. They did not obey the king of Egypt’s order; they kept the boys alive. So the king of Egypt sent for the midwives and demanded, “Why have you acted like this, keeping the boys alive?” The midwives told Pharaoh, “Hebrew women are different from Egyptian women. They are strong and quick, and they have their babies before the midwife gets there.” So God was good to the midwives, and the people kept growing in number and became very strong. And because the midwives feared God, he provided them with households of their own. Then Pharaoh gave an order to all his people: “Every boy that is born must be thrown into the Nile, but every girl is to be spared.”

fields.title: Exodus 2
fields.body_html:
Moses’ birth and flight to Midian

A man from the family of Levi married a woman who was also a descendant of Levi. She became pregnant and gave birth to a son. She saw how fine a child he was, and for three months she kept him hidden. When she could not hide him any longer, she made him a small ark out of papyrus reeds and sealed it with bitumen and pitch. She laid the child inside and set it among the reeds at the edge of the Nile. His sister took up a position some way off to find out what would become of him. Pharaoh’s daughter came down to the Nile to bathe, while her young women walked along the riverside. Catching sight of the ark among the reeds, she sent her servant girl to fetch it. She opened it and saw the child, a baby boy, and he was crying. She took pity on him. “This must be one of the Hebrews’ children,” she said. Then his sister asked Pharaoh’s daughter, “Would you like me to go and find you a Hebrew woman who can nurse the child for you?” “Go,” Pharaoh’s daughter told her. So the girl went and brought the child’s own mother. Pharaoh’s daughter said to her, “Take this child with you and nurse him for me. I will pay you for it.” So the woman took the child away and nursed him. When the child was older, his mother brought him to Pharaoh’s daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, “because,” she said, “I pulled him out of the water.” Years later, when Moses was a grown man, he went out to his own people and saw for himself their heavy labor. He saw an Egyptian beating a Hebrew, one of his own kinsmen. He glanced around in every direction, and when he saw no one there, he struck the Egyptian dead and buried him in the sand. The next day he went out again and found two Hebrews fighting each other. He said to the one who was at fault, “Why are you beating your neighbor?” The man answered, “Who put you in charge of us as ruler and judge? Do you intend to kill me the way you killed the Egyptian?” Then Moses was afraid. “So it is known what I did,” he thought. When Pharaoh heard about it, he tried to have Moses put to death. But Moses escaped from Pharaoh and settled in the land of Midian. There he sat down beside a well. The priest of Midian had seven daughters. They came to draw water and fill the troughs for their father’s flock to drink. But some shepherds came and chased them off. Moses stood up and defended them, and he watered their flock. When the girls came home to Reuel their father, he asked, “How is it that you are back so soon today?” “An Egyptian came to our defense against the shepherds,” they answered. “He even drew water for us himself and watered the flock.” He said to his daughters, “Where is he, then? Why did you leave the man behind? Go and ask him to come and share our meal.” Moses was content to live with the man, and the man gave Moses his daughter Zipporah as his wife. She gave birth to a son, and Moses called him Gershom. “I have lived as an outsider in a foreign country,” he said.

God hears Israel’s groaning

A long time passed, and the king of Egypt died. The Israelites groaned under their slavery and cried out, and their plea for help rose up to God from their bondage. God heard how they groaned, and God remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God looked upon the Israelites, and God took notice.

fields.title: Exodus 3
fields.body_html:
Moses at the burning bush

Moses was looking after the flock of his father-in-law Jethro, the priest of Midian. He led the flock deep into the wilderness and came to Horeb, the mountain of God. There the angel of the LORD appeared to him in a flame of fire coming out of a bush. Moses looked, and although the bush was ablaze, it was not burning away. Moses said, “I must turn aside and look at this remarkable sight. Why is the bush not burning away?” When the LORD saw that he had come over to look, God called out to him from the bush: “Moses! Moses!” “Yes, I am here,” he answered. “Come no nearer,” God said. “Remove your sandals from your feet, because the place where you stand is holy ground.” Then God said, “I am the God your father worshiped, the God of Abraham, of Isaac, and of Jacob.” Moses covered his face, for he was afraid to look upon God. The LORD said, “I have taken full note of the misery of my people in Egypt. I have heard them cry out under their taskmasters. I know how they are suffering. I have come down to rescue them from the power of Egypt and to lead them up out of that country into a fine, wide land, a land flowing with milk and honey, where the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites now live. The outcry of the Israelites has now reached me, and I have seen how harshly the Egyptians are crushing them. Go, then. I will send you to Pharaoh, and you are to bring my people, the Israelites, out of Egypt.” But Moses said to God, “Who am I to go to Pharaoh, and to bring the Israelites out of Egypt?” God answered, “I will be with you. And this will be your proof that I am the one who sent you: when you have brought the people out of Egypt, you will all worship God here on this mountain.” Moses said to God, “Suppose I go to the Israelites and tell them, ‘The God of your fathers has sent me to you,’ and they ask me, ‘What is his name?’ What answer am I to give them?” God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.” And he said, “Tell the Israelites this: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God also told Moses, “Say this to the Israelites: ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, has sent me to you.’ That is my name for all time, the name by which I am to be remembered in every generation. Go and call together the elders of Israel and tell them, ‘The LORD, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, appeared to me. He said, “I have come to your aid, and I have taken note of how you are treated in Egypt. I have resolved to lead you up from your suffering in Egypt to the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, a land flowing with milk and honey.”‘ They will listen to you. Then you and the elders of Israel are to go to the king of Egypt and say to him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, has come to meet us. Now please allow us to make a three-day journey into the wilderness to offer sacrifice to the LORD our God.’ I know, though, that the king of Egypt will not let you go unless he is forced by a mighty hand. So I will reach out my hand and strike Egypt with every kind of wonder that I will do there. Then at last he will send you away. I will make the Egyptians look kindly on this people, so that when you leave, you will not go away with nothing. Every woman is to ask her Egyptian neighbor, and any woman lodging in her house, for silver and gold jewelry and for clothing. You will dress your sons and daughters in them, and so you will strip Egypt of its wealth.”

fields.title: Exodus 4
fields.body_html:
Signs for Moses

Moses replied, “But they will not trust me or pay attention to what I say. They will say, ‘The LORD never appeared to you.’” The LORD asked him, “What is that you are holding?” “A staff,” he answered. God said, “Throw it down on the ground.” So Moses threw it down, and it turned into a snake, and he ran away from it. Then the LORD told Moses, “Reach out and catch it by the tail.” He reached out and grasped it, and it became a staff again in his hand. “This is so that they will believe that the LORD has appeared to you, the God of their fathers, the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.” The LORD spoke to him again: “Put your hand inside the fold of your robe.” Moses did so, and when he drew it out, his hand was diseased, white as snow. “Now put your hand back inside your robe,” God said. Moses put it back, and when he took it out, it was healthy again like the rest of his body. “If they do not believe you or are not convinced by the first sign, the second sign may persuade them. But if they still do not believe, even after these two signs, and will not listen to you, draw some water from the Nile and pour it out on dry land. The water you draw from the river will become blood there on the land.” Then Moses said to the LORD, “Please, Lord, I have never been a good speaker, not in the past, and not since you began speaking to your servant. My mouth is slow and my tongue is clumsy.” The LORD answered him, “Who gave human beings a mouth? Who makes a person unable to speak or hear, or able to see, or blind? Is it not I, the LORD? So go now. I will be with your mouth, and I will teach you what you are to say.” But Moses said, “Please, Lord, send someone else, whoever you choose.” Then the LORD became angry with Moses and said, “What about Aaron the Levite, your brother? I know he is a fluent speaker. In fact he is setting out now to meet you, and his heart will be full of joy when he sees you. You will talk to him and give him the words to say. I will be with you both as you speak, and I will show you what to do. He will speak to the people for you. He will be your spokesman, and you will be like God to him. And take this staff in your hand. You will use it to do the signs.”

Moses returns to Egypt

Moses went back to his father-in-law Jethro and said, “Please let me return to my own people in Egypt to find out whether they are still living.” Jethro told Moses, “Go, and may all be well with you.” The LORD said to Moses in Midian, “Go back to Egypt. All those who wanted you dead have died themselves.” So Moses took his wife and his sons, put them on a donkey, and set out for the land of Egypt. In his hand he carried the staff of God. The LORD told Moses, “When you go back to Egypt, be sure to do in Pharaoh’s presence all the wonders I have given you power to perform. But I will make his heart stubborn, and he will refuse to let the people go. Then tell Pharaoh, ‘The LORD says this: Israel is my firstborn son. I have told you, “Let my son go, so that he may worship me.” But you have refused to release him. Now I am going to put your firstborn son to death.’” On the way, at a place where they stopped for the night, the LORD confronted Moses and was about to kill him. But Zipporah took a sharp flint and cut off her son’s foreskin. She touched Moses’ feet with it and said, “You are a bridegroom of blood to me!” So the LORD let him go. It was then that she said, “A bridegroom of blood,” referring to the circumcision.

Aaron meets Moses

The LORD said to Aaron, “Go out into the wilderness to meet Moses.” So he went, and he met him at the mountain of God and greeted him with a kiss. Moses reported to Aaron all the words the LORD had sent him with, and all the signs he had ordered him to perform. Moses and Aaron went and called together all the elders of the Israelites. Aaron repeated all that the LORD had said to Moses, and he performed the signs in the people’s sight. And the people believed. When they heard that the LORD had come to help the Israelites and had seen their suffering, they bowed low and worshiped.

fields.title: Exodus 5
fields.body_html:
Bricks without straw

After that, Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and told him, “The LORD, the God of Israel, says, ‘Release my people so that they can celebrate a festival for me in the wilderness.’” Pharaoh replied, “Who is the LORD, that I should do what he says and release Israel? I do not know the LORD, and I will certainly not let Israel go.” They said, “The God of the Hebrews has come to meet us. Please let us travel three days into the wilderness to offer sacrifice to the LORD our God, or he may strike us down with disease or war.” The king of Egypt answered them, “Moses and Aaron, why are you distracting the people from their tasks? Get back to your labor!” Pharaoh went on, “Look how numerous these people of the land have become, and you want to give them rest from their labor!” That same day Pharaoh gave orders to the taskmasters over the people and to their foremen: “Do not supply the people with straw for brickmaking any longer, as you have been doing. Let them go out and collect their own straw. But require of them the same number of bricks as before; do not lower the quota. They are idle, which is why they keep calling out, ‘Let us go and sacrifice to our God.’ Make the work heavier for these men; keep them busy at it so that they will not listen to lies.” So the taskmasters and foremen went out and announced to the people, “Pharaoh says, ‘I will give you no more straw. Go and get straw for yourselves wherever you can find it. But your workload will not be reduced one bit.’” The people spread out over the whole land of Egypt to gather stubble to use as straw. The taskmasters kept up the pressure: “Finish your work, each day’s quota on its day, just as you did when straw was supplied.” The Israelite foremen whom Pharaoh’s taskmasters had put in charge were beaten and asked, “Why have you not made your full quota of bricks, either yesterday or today, as you did before?” Then the Israelite foremen went and appealed to Pharaoh: “Why do you treat your servants like this? No straw is given to your servants, and still they say to us, ‘Make bricks!’ Now your servants are beaten, though it is your own people who are in the wrong.” But he answered, “You are idle, nothing but idle! That is why you keep saying, ‘Let us go and offer sacrifice to the LORD.’ Now go and work. You will be given no straw, but you must still turn in the full count of bricks.” The Israelite foremen knew they were in serious trouble when they were told, “You must not reduce your daily count of bricks.” As they came out from Pharaoh’s presence, they found Moses and Aaron standing there waiting for them. They said to them, “May the LORD see what you have done and judge you! You have made us hateful to Pharaoh and his officials, and you have handed them a sword to kill us.” Moses turned back to the LORD and said, “Lord, why have you brought this evil on this people? Why did you send me at all? From the moment I went to speak to Pharaoh in your name, he has treated this people cruelly, and you have done nothing at all to rescue your people.”

fields.title: Exodus 6
fields.body_html:
God promises to bring Israel out

The LORD answered Moses, “Now you are going to see what I will do to Pharaoh. Compelled by a strong hand, he will release them; compelled by a strong hand, he will drive them from his land.”

God spoke to Moses and told him, “I am the LORD. I showed myself to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as God Almighty, but I did not make myself known to them by my name, the LORD. I also confirmed my covenant with them, that I would give them the land of Canaan, the land where they stayed as foreigners. I myself have now heard the Israelites groaning under the slavery the Egyptians force on them, and I have kept my covenant in mind. So tell the Israelites: ‘I am the LORD. I will lead you out from under the forced labor of the Egyptians and rescue you from serving them as slaves. I will redeem you with my arm stretched out and with great acts of judgment. I will claim you as a people for me, and I will be your God. And you will know that I am the LORD your God, the one who brings you out from under the forced labor of Egypt. I will bring you into the land that I promised with an oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and I will give it to you to hold as your own. I am the LORD.’” Moses passed this on to the Israelites, but they would not listen to him. Their spirits were worn down and their slavery was cruel.

Moses sent again to Pharaoh

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and tell him to release the Israelites from his country.” But Moses answered the LORD, “Even the Israelites have not listened to me. How can I expect Pharaoh to listen, when I speak so poorly?”

The LORD spoke to Moses and Aaron and gave them a charge for the Israelites and for Pharaoh, king of Egypt: they were to bring the Israelites out of the land of Egypt.

The family lines of Moses and Aaron

Here are the heads of the family lines. Reuben was Israel’s firstborn; his sons were Hanoch, Pallu, Hezron, and Carmi. These were the Reubenite clans. The sons of Simeon were Jemuel, Jamin, Ohad, Jakin, Zohar, and Shaul, whose mother was a Canaanite. These were the Simeonite clans. These are the names of Levi’s sons, by their family lines: Gershon, Kohath, and Merari. Levi lived 137 years. Gershon’s sons were Libni and Shimei, each with his clan. Kohath’s sons were Amram, Izhar, Hebron, and Uzziel. Kohath lived 133 years. Merari’s sons were Mahli and Mushi. These were the clans of Levi, listed by their family lines. Amram took as his wife Jochebed, the sister of his father, and she bore him Aaron and Moses. The length of Amram’s life was 137 years. Izhar’s sons were Korah, Nepheg, and Zikri. Uzziel’s sons were Mishael, Elzaphan, and Sithri. Aaron married Elisheba, daughter of Amminadab and sister of Nahshon, and she bore him Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar. Korah’s sons were Assir, Elkanah, and Abiasaph. These were the Korahite clans. Eleazar son of Aaron married one of Putiel’s daughters, and she bore him Phinehas. These were the heads of the Levite families, clan by clan. This Aaron and this Moses are the ones the LORD told, “Lead the Israelites out of the land of Egypt, company by company.” It was they who went before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and spoke to him so that the Israelites might be brought out of Egypt: this Moses and this Aaron. Now on the day when the LORD spoke to Moses in the land of Egypt,

the LORD said to Moses, “I am the LORD. Repeat to Pharaoh, king of Egypt, every word I speak to you.” But Moses replied in the presence of the LORD, “I am such a poor speaker. How will Pharaoh ever listen to me?”

fields.title: Exodus 7
fields.body_html:
Moses and Aaron before Pharaoh

The LORD said to Moses, “See, I have appointed you to be as God to Pharaoh, and your brother Aaron will serve as your prophet. Say everything I give you to say. Then your brother Aaron will speak to Pharaoh, so that he lets the Israelites leave his land. As for me, I will make Pharaoh’s heart hard, and I will fill the land of Egypt with my signs and wonders. Pharaoh will not listen to you. Then I will set my hand against Egypt and, with great judgments, lead my ranks, my people the Israelites, out of the land of Egypt. When I reach out my hand against Egypt and lead the Israelites out from among its people, the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.” So Moses and Aaron obeyed; they did just what the LORD told them. At the time they spoke to Pharaoh, Moses was eighty years old, and Aaron was eighty-three.

Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent

The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “If Pharaoh demands, ‘Prove yourselves with a wonder,’ tell Aaron to take his staff and throw it down in front of Pharaoh. It will turn into a serpent.” Moses and Aaron went to Pharaoh and did as the LORD had commanded. Aaron cast his staff to the ground before Pharaoh and his court, and it turned into a serpent. Pharaoh in turn called for his wise men and sorcerers, and the magicians of Egypt did the same thing with their spells. Every one of them threw his staff to the ground, and these too became serpents. Then Aaron’s staff swallowed theirs. But Pharaoh’s heart remained stubborn. He refused to listen to them, as the LORD had said he would.

The Nile turns to blood

The LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh is stubborn at heart and will not release the people. Go to Pharaoh in the morning, when he goes out to the water. Wait for him on the bank of the Nile, and have in your hand the staff that turned into a snake. Say to him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, sent me to tell you, “Release my people, so they can serve me in the wilderness.” So far, you have refused to listen. This is what the LORD says: “Here is how you will know that I am the LORD: I am about to strike the Nile’s water with this staff in my hand, and it will become blood. Its fish will die, the Nile will smell foul, and the Egyptians will be unable to stomach its water.”‘”

The LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Take your staff and hold out your hand over the waters of Egypt, over its branches of the Nile, its canals, its marshes, and every place where its water is collected, so that they become blood.’ Blood will be found all through the land of Egypt, even in vessels of wood and of stone.” Moses and Aaron did as the LORD had commanded. While Pharaoh and his officials watched, he lifted up the staff and struck the water of the Nile, and all the water in the river was turned into blood. The Nile’s fish died and the river began to reek; the Egyptians could not drink from it. Throughout the land of Egypt there was blood. But the magicians of Egypt did the same with their spells, and Pharaoh’s heart stayed stubborn. He did not listen to them; it happened as the LORD had said. Pharaoh turned his back and went into his palace, giving no thought even to this. Unable to drink the water of the Nile, all the Egyptians dug around the river to find water fit to drink. After the LORD had struck the Nile, seven full days passed.

fields.title: Exodus 8
fields.body_html:
A warning of frogs

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘The LORD says this: “Release my people, so they can serve me. If you refuse to let them go, watch: I will strike your whole country with frogs. The Nile will swarm with frogs. They will climb out and get into your palace, into the room where you sleep and onto your bed, into your officials’ houses and onto your people, into your ovens and the bowls you knead dough in.

Frogs cover the land

On you, on your people, and on all your officials the frogs will climb.”‘” The LORD said to Moses, “Tell Aaron, ‘Hold out your hand with your staff over the rivers, the canals, and the pools, and bring the frogs up over the land of Egypt.’” So Aaron held his hand out over the waters of Egypt. The frogs came up and covered the land of Egypt. The magicians matched this with their spells and brought frogs up onto the land of Egypt as well. Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said, “Plead with the LORD to rid me and my people of the frogs, and I will release the people so they can offer sacrifice to the LORD.” Moses said to Pharaoh, “The choice is yours, and the honor: say when I should pray for you, your officials, and your people, and the frogs will be cut off from you and your houses. They will stay only in the Nile.” Pharaoh answered, “Tomorrow.” Moses said, “Then it will be done at your word, and you will learn that the LORD our God has no equal. The frogs will go away from you, from your houses, from your officials, and from your people. Only in the Nile will any be left.” Moses and Aaron went out from Pharaoh’s presence, and Moses called out to the LORD about the frogs that he had sent against Pharaoh. The LORD granted Moses’ request. In the houses, the courtyards, and the fields, the frogs died off. People gathered them into great heaps, and the land stank. Once Pharaoh saw that he had breathing room, he hardened his heart. He would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said.

Gnats

The LORD told Moses, “Tell Aaron to hold out his staff and strike the dust on the ground. Throughout the land of Egypt the dust will turn into gnats.” So they did it. When Aaron raised his staff in his hand and struck the dust of the ground, gnats were on people and animals alike. Across the whole land of Egypt, all the dust turned into gnats. The magicians attempted the same with their spells, to bring out gnats, but they failed. And still the gnats were on people and animals. The magicians told Pharaoh, “This is the finger of God at work!” But Pharaoh’s heart stayed stubborn, and he refused to listen to them, as the LORD had said.

Swarms of flies

The LORD said to Moses, “Be up early in the morning and take your stand in front of Pharaoh as he comes out to the water. Say to him, ‘The LORD says this: Release my people so that they can serve me. If you do not let my people go, I will send swarms of flies against you, your officials, your people, and your houses. The houses of the Egyptians will be filled with the swarms, and so will the very ground where they live. On that day, though, I will set apart Goshen, the region where my people live: no flies will swarm there. That way you will learn that I, the LORD, am right here in the land. I will make a rescue that sets my people apart from your people. Tomorrow the sign will come.’” The LORD carried this out. Great swarms of flies invaded Pharaoh’s house and his officials’ houses. Across the whole land of Egypt, the flies brought ruin to the land. Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said, “Go and offer sacrifices to your God, but do it here in this land.” Moses answered, “It would not be fitting to do that. The sacrifices we offer to the LORD our God are offensive to the Egyptians. If we offered, right in front of them, sacrifices they find offensive, they would stone us, would they not? We will travel for three days into the wilderness, and there we will sacrifice to the LORD our God, as he instructs us.” Pharaoh said, “Very well, I will release you, and you may sacrifice to the LORD your God in the wilderness. Just do not travel too far away. And pray on my behalf.” Moses said, “I am leaving you now, and I will plead with the LORD. Tomorrow the flies will depart from Pharaoh, from his officials, and from his people. But Pharaoh must not trick us again and keep the people from going to sacrifice to the LORD.” Moses went out from Pharaoh’s presence and prayed to the LORD. The LORD answered Moses’ request and took the flies away from Pharaoh, his officials, and his people. Not a single one was left. Yet once again Pharaoh hardened his heart; he did not release the people.

fields.title: Exodus 9
fields.body_html:
Disease strikes the livestock

The LORD said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh and tell him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says this: Release my people, so they can serve me. If you refuse to let them go and keep your grip on them, then the hand of the LORD will fall on your animals out in the fields, on your horses, donkeys, and camels, your cattle and your sheep, with a very severe disease. But the LORD will set Israel’s livestock apart from Egypt’s, and not one animal that belongs to the Israelites will die.’” The LORD fixed a time and said, “Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land.” The LORD carried this out on the following day. Egypt’s livestock all died, but of the livestock of the Israelites not one animal was lost. Pharaoh sent men to look into it, and indeed not a single animal of Israel’s livestock had died. Yet Pharaoh stayed stubborn and did not release the people.

Boils

The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “Fill both your hands with soot from a kiln, and let Moses throw it up toward the sky in Pharaoh’s sight. It will turn into fine dust over the whole land of Egypt, and all through the land it will become boils, bursting into blisters on people and on animals.” They took the kiln soot and went to stand in front of Pharaoh. When Moses threw it up toward the sky, it became boils, breaking out in blisters on people and animals alike. The boils kept the magicians from even appearing before Moses, for they had the boils, as did all the Egyptians. The LORD, however, hardened the heart of Pharaoh, who refused to listen to them, as the LORD had told Moses.

A warning of hail

The LORD said to Moses, “Be up early in the morning and take your stand in front of Pharaoh. Tell him, ‘The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says this: Release my people, so they can serve me. For now I will aim all my plagues at your very heart, and at your officials and your people. Then you will learn that in the whole world there is none like me. I could already have raised my hand and struck you and your people with deadly disease, and you would have disappeared from the earth. But I have let you survive for this purpose: to show you my power and to have my name declared throughout the earth. Even now you raise yourself up against my people, refusing to release them. About this time tomorrow I will rain down hail so heavy that Egypt has seen nothing like it from the day the nation began until now. So now send word to get your livestock and everything you have out in the open under cover. Any person or animal still in the fields and not brought indoors will die when the hail falls on them.’” Among Pharaoh’s officials, those who feared the word of the LORD made their servants and their livestock run for the houses. Others gave no thought to the word of the LORD and left their servants and livestock out in the open.

Hail strikes Egypt

The LORD told Moses, “Raise your hand toward the sky so that hail comes down all over the land of Egypt, striking people, animals, and every green plant in Egypt’s fields.” Moses held his staff up toward the sky, and the LORD sent out peals of thunder and hail. Lightning streaked down to the earth while the LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt. Hail fell, with lightning flaring through the middle of it. The hail was very heavy, worse than any the whole land of Egypt had known since it became a nation. All across the land of Egypt, whatever was out in the fields, human or animal, was struck by the hail. The hail flattened every plant in the fields and splintered every tree. Only in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, was there no hail. Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said to them, “I have sinned this time. The LORD is in the right, and the guilt lies with me and my people. Plead with the LORD. There has been enough of God’s thunder and hail. I will release you. You will stay here no longer.” Moses replied, “As soon as I am outside the city, I will spread my hands out toward the LORD. Then the thunder will end and the hail will be gone, and you will learn that the earth belongs to the LORD. But you and your officials, I know, have yet to fear the LORD God.” The flax and barley crops were lost, because the barley had already headed out and the flax had come into flower. The wheat and spelt escaped, since they are later crops. So Moses left Pharaoh and went outside the city, where he spread his hands out toward the LORD. The thunder and hail came to an end, and the rain stopped pouring onto the ground. Once Pharaoh saw that rain, hail, and thunder had all ceased, he went back to sinning: he hardened his heart, and so did his officials. Pharaoh remained stubborn and refused to release the Israelites. It was as the LORD had foretold through Moses.

fields.title: Exodus 10
fields.body_html:
A warning of locusts

The LORD said to Moses, “Go in to Pharaoh. It is I who have hardened his heart and the hearts of his officials, in order to set these signs of mine right among them, and so that you can tell your children and grandchildren the story of how I made a mockery of Egypt, and of the signs I set among them. And you will all know that I am the LORD.” So Moses and Aaron went in to Pharaoh and told him, “The LORD, the God of the Hebrews, says this: ‘How long will you go on refusing to bow before me? Release my people, so that they can serve me. If you refuse to release my people, then tomorrow I will bring locusts across your borders. They will blanket the face of the land until no one can see the ground. They will consume whatever the hail spared, all that you still have left, and they will feed on every tree of yours that grows in the open country. Your houses will be full of them, and so will the houses of all your officials and of all the Egyptians. It will be a sight your ancestors never saw, neither your fathers nor their fathers, in all the time they have lived on this soil.’” Then Moses turned and went out from Pharaoh’s presence. Pharaoh’s officials said to him, “How long must this man be a trap for us? Let the men go and serve the LORD their God. Have you still not grasped that Egypt is lost?” Moses and Aaron were brought back to Pharaoh, who said to them, “Go and serve the LORD your God. But exactly who will be going?” Moses said, “Young and old alike, we will go. Our sons and daughters will go, and our flocks and herds too, for we are holding a festival of the LORD.” Pharaoh said to them, “So the LORD be with you, just as surely as I will let you go with your little ones! Plainly you are plotting harm. Not that way! You men may go and serve the LORD; that, after all, is what you want.” With that, they were driven away from Pharaoh.

Locusts cover the land

The LORD said to Moses, “Hold out your hand over the land of Egypt to bring the locusts. They will come up over the land of Egypt and eat every plant in the country, everything the hail left standing.” So Moses held out his staff over the land of Egypt, and the LORD sent an east wind blowing over the land all that day and all that night. When morning came, the locusts were there, borne in on the east wind. The locusts swept over the whole land of Egypt and settled throughout its territory in vast numbers. No locust swarm before it had ever been like this one, and none after it will be. They covered the face of the whole land until the land went dark. They ate up every plant in the country and all the fruit on the trees that the hail had spared. Across the whole land of Egypt, no tree and no field plant kept a single green leaf. Pharaoh hastily sent for Moses and Aaron. He said, “I have sinned against the LORD your God, and against you too. Now please forgive my sin, just this once. Plead with the LORD your God to lift this death from me, if nothing more.” Moses went out from Pharaoh’s presence and prayed to the LORD. Then the LORD turned the wind around. A gale blew in from the west, lifted the locusts, and swept them into the Red Sea. In all the territory of Egypt not one locust remained. Yet the LORD made Pharaoh stubborn, and he did not release the Israelites.

Three days of darkness

The LORD said to Moses, “Raise your hand toward the sky, and darkness will come over the land of Egypt, a darkness so thick that people can feel it.” So Moses raised his hand toward the sky, and deep darkness lay over the whole land of Egypt for three days. For three days nobody could see anybody else, and nobody stirred from where they were. But the Israelites all had light in their homes. Pharaoh summoned Moses and said, “Go and serve the LORD. Only your flocks and herds are to be kept back; even your little ones may go along with you.” Moses said, “You yourself must even put into our hands sacrifices and burnt offerings for us to offer to the LORD our God. Our animals are coming with us too; not a single hoof will stay behind. It is from them that we must take what we use to serve the LORD our God, and until we reach the place, we ourselves cannot tell which ones we will need to serve the LORD.” But the LORD made Pharaoh stubborn, and he would not agree to let them go. Pharaoh said to him, “Out of my sight! Watch yourself: do not come before me ever again. If you see my face one more time, that day you will die.” Moses said, “You are right. This is the last time I will see your face.”

fields.title: Exodus 11
fields.body_html:
One plague still to come

The LORD said to Moses, “There is one plague still to come. I will bring it on Pharaoh and on Egypt, and after it he will let you leave this place. When he lets you go, he will drive you out of here for good. Now tell the people, so that all of them hear it, that each man is to ask his Egyptian neighbor, and each woman hers, for articles of silver and gold.” The LORD made the Egyptians look kindly on the people. Moses, too, was a very great man in the land of Egypt; Pharaoh’s officials and the people looked on him with respect.

Moses warns of the death of the firstborn

Moses then told Pharaoh, “The LORD says this: ‘Around midnight I am going out into the heart of Egypt. Every firstborn in the land of Egypt will die, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, seated on his throne, to the firstborn of the female servant who grinds grain at the millstones, and every firstborn of the animals as well. A great cry of grief will go up across the whole land of Egypt. Nothing like it has happened before, and nothing like it will happen again. But among the Israelites not even a dog will snarl at anyone, human or animal. So you will know that the LORD sets Israel apart from Egypt.’ Every one of these officials of yours will come down to me and bow to the ground, and they will say, ‘Leave, you and all the people at your heels!’ Only then will I go.” And Moses walked out from Pharaoh’s presence in fierce anger.

The LORD said to Moses, “Pharaoh will not heed you, so that I may do still more wonders in the land of Egypt.” Moses and Aaron did all these wonders in front of Pharaoh, but the LORD made Pharaoh’s heart stubborn, and he did not release the Israelites from his land.

fields.title: Exodus 12
fields.body_html:
The Passover

In the land of Egypt, the LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “From now on this month is to head your calendar: count it as the first month of your year. Speak to the whole community of Israel and tell them: ‘On the tenth day of this month the head of every family is to pick out a lamb, one lamb to a household. Should a household be too small for a whole lamb, the man is to join with the neighbor who lives closest and take one between them, counting the people in both homes. Divide the lamb by how much each one will eat. It must be a sound, unblemished male in its first year, picked from either the sheep or the goats. Look after it until the fourteenth day of this month. On that day, as evening falls, the whole assembled community of Israel is to slaughter their lambs. Some of the blood is to go on the two doorposts and on the lintel of each house where the lamb is eaten. The meat is to be eaten that night, fire-roasted, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. None of it is to be eaten raw or stewed in water. It must be roasted in the fire whole, with its head, its legs, and its inner organs. None of it may be kept until morning; whatever is still uneaten at daybreak must be burned in the fire. When you eat it, be ready to set out: robes tucked into your belts, sandals on, staffs in hand. Eat it quickly. It is the LORD’s Passover. This very night I will go through the land of Egypt and strike down every firstborn in it, human and animal alike. Against all the gods of Egypt I will carry out judgments. I am the LORD. The blood will mark the houses where you are staying; it will be a sign for you. I will see the blood and pass over you, and the plague that destroys will not fall on you when I strike the land of Egypt. This day is to be one you remember. Hold a feast to the LORD on it, generation after generation, as a statute for all time. Unleavened bread is to be your food for seven days. On the first day, without fail, rid your houses of leaven. Anyone who eats leavened bread at any time from the first day to the seventh will be cut off from Israel. The first day and the seventh day are each to be a holy convocation for you, days when no work is done. The only work allowed is getting food ready, so that everyone can eat. Observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread, since this is the very day I led your ranks out of the land of Egypt. Keep this day in every generation as a statute for all time. From the evening of the fourteenth day of the first month to the evening of the twenty-first, you are to eat unleavened bread. For seven days there must be no leaven anywhere in your houses. Anyone who eats food made with leaven will be cut off from the community of Israel, whether a foreigner living among you or one born in the land. Nothing leavened is to be eaten; in every place where you live, your bread is to be unleavened.’”

Moses instructs the elders

So Moses summoned all the elders of Israel. “Go and choose lambs from the flock, one for each of your clans,” he told them, “and slaughter the Passover lamb. Dip a bundle of hyssop into the blood in the basin, and with it brush the blood onto the lintel and the two doorposts. Then no one is to step outside the house until morning. The LORD will pass through to strike Egypt, and when he sees the blood on the lintel and on both doorposts, he will pass over that doorway and not allow the destroyer into your houses to strike you. You and your descendants are to keep this command as a statute for all time. And once you have come into the land that the LORD will give you, just as he has said, you are to go on keeping this service. In time your children will say to you, ‘What is this service of yours about?’ Then you are to tell them, ‘This is the sacrifice of the LORD’s Passover. When he struck Egypt, he passed over the houses of the Israelites there and rescued our homes.’” At this the people bowed low and worshiped. Then the Israelites went and did it. They did exactly as the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.

Every firstborn is struck down

In the middle of the night the LORD struck down every firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, the king on his throne, down to the firstborn of the captive locked in the dungeon, along with every firstborn among the animals. Pharaoh got up in the night, and so did all his officials and every Egyptian. A great cry of grief went up across Egypt, because no house was without its dead. While it was still night, Pharaoh sent for Moses and Aaron and said, “Up! Get out from among my people, you and the Israelites with you! Go and serve the LORD, as you have been saying. Take your flocks and your herds as well, as you demanded, and be gone. And ask a blessing for me too.” The Egyptians pressed the people to leave the land with all speed. “We are as good as dead, every one of us!” they said. So the people picked up their dough before it had a chance to rise and carried it on their shoulders, the kneading bowls tied up in their cloaks. The Israelites acted on Moses’ word: they asked the Egyptians for articles of silver and gold, and for clothing. The LORD had made the Egyptians look kindly on the people, and they granted what was asked. So Israel stripped Egypt of its wealth.

Israel leaves Egypt

The Israelites set out from Rameses for Succoth. There were about 600,000 men on foot, not counting the little ones. A large crowd of people of mixed descent went with them as well, and great numbers of animals, flocks and herds alike. From the dough they had carried out of Egypt they baked flat cakes of unleavened bread. It had not risen, since they had been driven out of Egypt with no chance to linger, and they had not got any food ready for the road. The time the Israelites spent living in Egypt came to 430 years. When the 430 years were over, on that very same day, all the ranks of the LORD marched out of the land of Egypt. That was a night when the LORD kept watch, so as to bring them out of the land of Egypt. This same night belongs to the LORD, and all the Israelites are to keep watch on it, generation after generation.

Who may eat the Passover

The LORD said to Moses and Aaron, “This is the statute for the Passover. No foreigner is to eat of it. A slave bought with money may share in it, but only after you have circumcised him. Neither a settler nor a hired laborer is to eat it. It is to be eaten within one house. No meat is to be carried outside the house, and you must not break a bone of it. The whole community of Israel is to keep it. Suppose a foreigner living among you wants to hold a Passover for the LORD. Every male in his household must first be circumcised. Then he may come near and keep it, and he will count as one born in the land. But anyone uncircumcised is not to eat of it. One law is to govern both the native-born and the foreigner living among you.” All the Israelites carried out exactly what the LORD had commanded Moses and Aaron.

On that same day the LORD led the Israelites out of the land of Egypt, company by company.

fields.title: Exodus 13
fields.body_html:
Firstborn and unleavened bread

The LORD said to Moses, “Set apart as holy to me every firstborn among the Israelites, each one that comes first from its mother’s womb, human and animal alike. It belongs to me.” Moses said to the people, “Remember this day, the day you came out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. The LORD brought you out of this place by the strength of his hand. No leavened bread may be eaten. You are going out today, in the month of Abib. When the LORD brings you into the land of the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Hivites, and Jebusites, the land he swore to your ancestors that he would give you, a land flowing with milk and honey, you are to perform this rite in this same month. You are to eat unleavened bread for seven days, and the seventh day is a feast in honor of the LORD. Throughout the seven days unleavened bread is to be eaten. No leavened bread may be found among you, and no leaven anywhere in all your territory. On that day tell your son what it means: ‘The LORD acted for me when I left Egypt, and that is why we do this.’ This feast will be a sign for you, like a mark on your hand, and a reminder, like a mark between your eyes, so that the instruction of the LORD stays on your lips. For with a strong hand the LORD brought you out of Egypt. So you are to keep this statute at its proper time every year.

Redeeming the firstborn

Once the LORD has brought you into the land of the Canaanites and handed it over to you, as he swore he would to you and to your ancestors, then you must hand over to the LORD every firstborn that opens the womb. Every firstling born to your animals that is a male belongs to the LORD. Every firstborn donkey you are to redeem by giving a lamb in its place; if you will not redeem it, you must break its neck. And you are to redeem every firstborn son of yours. Later on, when your son asks you, ‘What is this?’ you shall answer him, ‘By the strength of his hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. When Pharaoh hardened himself against letting us go, the LORD killed every firstborn in the land of Egypt, the firstborn of people and of animals alike. So I offer to the LORD in sacrifice every male that first opens the womb, and I redeem each firstborn among my sons.’ It will be a sign for you, like a mark on your hand and a band between your eyes, for by the strength of his hand the LORD brought us out of Egypt.”

The pillar of cloud and fire

Once Pharaoh had sent the people away, God did not guide them along the route to the land of the Philistines, though it was the nearer way. For God thought, “The people may regret leaving when they find themselves facing war, and go back to Egypt.” Instead, God took the people the long way round, through the wilderness toward the Red Sea, and the Israelites left the land of Egypt equipped for battle. Moses brought Joseph’s bones along, since Joseph had bound the Israelites by a solemn oath. “God will certainly come to help you,” he had said, “and when he does, you are to take my bones up from here with you.” They moved on from Succoth and made camp at Etham, on the edge of the wilderness. The LORD went in front of them, in a pillar of cloud by day so that he could guide them along the way, and in a pillar of fire by night to light their path. In that way they could keep moving both day and night. By day the pillar of cloud, and by night the pillar of fire, never moved away from the front of the people.

fields.title: Exodus 14
fields.body_html:
Pharaoh chases Israel

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites to turn around and set up camp in front of Pi-hahiroth, between Migdol and the sea. Make your camp beside the sea, across from Baal-zephon. Pharaoh will say about the Israelites, ‘They are lost and wandering about the country; the wilderness has trapped them.’ I will make Pharaoh’s heart stubborn, and he will chase after them. Then I will win glory at the expense of Pharaoh and all his forces, and the Egyptians will know that I am the LORD.” The Israelites did as they were told. Word reached the king of Egypt that the people had run away, and Pharaoh and his officials turned against them. “Why did we do this?” they said. “We have let Israel go, and they will no longer serve us!” Then Pharaoh had his chariot harnessed and took his troops along. He took 600 picked chariots and the rest of Egypt’s chariot force too, with officers over the whole of it. The LORD made the heart of Pharaoh, king of Egypt, stubborn, and he went after the Israelites, who were leaving with heads held high. The Egyptians, all Pharaoh’s chariot horses, his horsemen and his army, went after them and caught up with them where they were camped by the sea, beside Pi-hahiroth, facing Baal-zephon. Pharaoh was drawing closer. When the Israelites looked up, they saw the Egyptians advancing behind them, and they were filled with fear. The Israelites cried out to the LORD. They said to Moses, “Did Egypt have no graves, that you had to bring us out here to die in the wilderness? What a thing to do to us, leading us out of Egypt! Did we not tell you this very thing back in Egypt? We said, ‘Let us be, and we will serve the Egyptians.’ Serving the Egyptians was better for us than dying here in the wilderness!” But Moses told the people, “Have no fear! Hold your ground and watch how the LORD will save you today. You see the Egyptians today, but you will never see them again. The LORD will fight on your behalf, and you can stay quiet.”

Crossing the sea on dry ground

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Why are you crying out to me? Tell the Israelites to break camp and go forward. As for you, lift up your staff, reach out your hand over the sea, and split it open, so that the Israelites can walk through the middle of the sea on dry ground. As for me, I am going to make the Egyptians stubborn, so that they follow them in. Then I will win glory at the expense of Pharaoh and his whole army, his chariots and his horsemen. The Egyptians will know that I am the LORD when I have won glory at the expense of Pharaoh, his chariots, and his horsemen.” The angel of God, who had been going ahead of Israel’s camp, moved and went to the rear, and the pillar of cloud moved from in front of them and took its place behind them. It came between the camp of Egypt and the camp of Israel. The cloud was there, and the darkness, and it lit up the night; and all night long neither camp approached the other. Moses held his hand out over the sea, and all night long the LORD pushed the sea back with a powerful east wind. He turned the sea into dry land, and the waters were split apart. The Israelites went into the middle of the sea on dry ground, and the water was a wall for them, to the right and to the left. The Egyptians gave chase and followed them into the middle of the sea, all Pharaoh’s horses, his chariots and his horsemen. In the last hours of the night, before morning, the LORD looked down on the Egyptian camp from the pillar of fire and cloud and threw the camp into panic. He made the wheels come off their chariots, so that they could hardly drive. Then the Egyptians said, “We must run from Israel, because the LORD is fighting on their side against Egypt!” The LORD said to Moses, “Hold your hand out over the sea, and the waters will flow back over the Egyptians, over their chariots and their horsemen.” So Moses held his hand out over the sea, and as morning broke the sea went back to its usual flow. The Egyptians were fleeing straight into it, and the LORD shook them off into the middle of the sea. The waters came back and covered the chariots and the horsemen, the whole of Pharaoh’s army that had followed Israel into the sea. Not a single one of them was left. The Israelites, though, walked on dry ground through the middle of the sea, with the water a wall for them to the right and to the left. So on that day the LORD saved Israel from the power of Egypt, and Israel saw the Egyptians dead along the edge of the sea. Israel had seen the great hand of the LORD at work against Egypt. So the people feared the LORD, and they believed in the LORD and in Moses, his servant.

fields.title: Exodus 15
fields.body_html:
The song of Moses

Then Moses and the Israelites sang this song to the LORD: “I will sing to the LORD, for he is lifted high in triumph; horse and rider he has flung into the sea. My strength and my song is the LORD; he has come to save me. This is my God, and I will honor him with praise; the God of my father, and I will lift him high. The LORD is a man of war; his name is the LORD. Pharaoh’s chariots and his army he has hurled into the sea; his finest officers went down in the Red Sea. The deep waters closed over them; like a stone they dropped to the bottom. O LORD, your right hand is splendid in power; O LORD, your right hand smashed the enemy. In your surpassing majesty you tore down those who rose against you; you let loose your fury, and it burned them up like straw. At the blast of your nostrils the waters were piled high; the flowing waters stood upright in a heap, and the depths grew solid in the heart of the sea. The enemy said, ‘I will chase them and catch them; I will share out the loot and take my fill of them; I will draw my sword, and my hand will wipe them out.’ But you breathed out, and the sea closed over them; they went down like lead in the powerful waters. Among the gods, who compares with you, O LORD? Who is like you, splendid in holiness, fearsome in deeds of praise, doer of wonders? You reached out your right hand, and the ground swallowed them. With faithful love you led the people you had redeemed; with your strength you guided them on to your holy abode. Nations heard and shuddered; agony took hold of those who lived in Philistia. Then Edom’s clan chiefs were struck with dismay; Moab’s rulers were gripped with trembling; everyone living in Canaan lost heart. Fear and dread came down on them; at the might of your arm they stood silent as stone, while your people crossed over, O LORD, while the people you made your own crossed over. You will bring them in and plant them on the mountain of your inheritance, the place you have prepared for your dwelling, O LORD, the sanctuary, O Lord, that your own hands set firm. The LORD will reign forever and ever!” Pharaoh’s horses, with his chariots and his horsemen, had gone into the sea, and the LORD had turned the sea’s waters back on top of them; but the Israelites had walked through the middle of the sea on dry ground.

Miriam’s song

Miriam the prophetess, Aaron’s sister, picked up a tambourine, and all the women came out behind her, beating tambourines and dancing. Miriam led them in the refrain: “Sing to the LORD, for he is lifted high in triumph; horse and rider he has flung into the sea.”

Bitter water at Marah

Moses had Israel move on from the Red Sea, and they went out into the wilderness of Shur. For three days they walked through the wilderness without coming upon any water. When they came to Marah, they could not drink the water there, because it was bitter. That is why the place was named Marah. The people grumbled at Moses. “What are we going to drink?” they said. Moses cried out to the LORD, and the LORD pointed him to a piece of wood. He threw it into the water, and the water turned sweet. It was there that the LORD laid down a statute and a rule for them, and there that he put them to the test. He said, “If you listen closely to the voice of the LORD your God and do what he sees as right, if you pay heed to his commands and keep all his statutes, I will spare you every one of the sicknesses that I laid on the Egyptians. For I am the LORD who heals you.”

Next they arrived at Elim. Twelve springs of water were there, and seventy palm trees, and they set up camp beside the water.

fields.title: Exodus 16
fields.body_html:
The people grumble for food
