After leaving Elim, the whole community of the Israelites arrived in the wilderness of Sin, between Elim and Sinai. It was the fifteenth day of the second month since they had come out of the land of Egypt. There in the wilderness the whole community of the Israelites grumbled against Moses and Aaron. The Israelites said to them, “We wish we had died at the hand of the LORD in the land of Egypt! There we sat beside the pots of meat and ate all the bread we could hold. But you two have brought us out into this wilderness to make this whole assembly die of hunger.”

The LORD said to Moses, “I am about to rain bread from heaven for you. Each day the people are to go out and gather the amount needed for that day. By this I will test them, to see whether they will live by my law or not. When they prepare on the sixth day what they have brought in, it will amount to double their usual daily gathering.”

Moses and Aaron told all the Israelites, “This evening you will come to know that it was the LORD who led you out of the land of Egypt, and in the morning you will see the glory of the LORD. For he has heard the grumbling you have aimed at the LORD. As for us, what are we? Why grumble against us?” Moses went on, “You will see this when the LORD gives you meat to eat in the evening, and bread in the morning until you are full, because the LORD has heard the grumbling you direct at him. What are we? Your grumbling is not aimed at us at all, but at the LORD.” Moses told Aaron to tell the whole community of the Israelites to come close and stand before the LORD, because he had heard their grumbling. While Aaron was still addressing the whole community of the Israelites, they turned to face the wilderness, and suddenly the glory of the LORD could be seen in the cloud.

Quail and bread from heaven

Then the LORD said to Moses, “The grumbling of the Israelites has reached my ears. Tell them this: ‘As evening falls you will eat meat, and in the morning you will have your fill of bread. Then you will know that I am the LORD your God.’” That evening, quail flew in and covered the camp, and by morning dew lay all around the camp. When the dew had lifted, the surface of the wilderness was covered with something fine and flaky, as thin as frost on the ground. “What is it?” the Israelites asked one another when they saw it, since they did not know what it was. Moses answered them, “It is bread, given to you by the LORD as your food. Here is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Each of you is to gather as much as you need to eat, about 2 quarts for every person. The head of each household is to collect it for everyone who lives in his tent.’” The Israelites did this. Some of them gathered a lot, and others only a little. Yet when they measured it with a 2-quart measure, the one who gathered much had nothing left over, and the one who gathered little had no shortage. All of them had gathered as much as they could eat. Moses told them, “None of you may save any of it for the next morning.” But they would not listen to Moses. Some people saved part of it until morning, and it became wormy and foul-smelling. This made Moses angry with them. So morning after morning they gathered it, everyone as much as they could eat, and when the heat of the sun came, what was left melted away. On the sixth day they gathered a double amount of bread, about 4 quarts per person. All the leaders of the community came and told Moses about it. He told them, “This is what the LORD said: ‘Tomorrow is a Sabbath rest, a holy Sabbath to the LORD.’ So today bake whatever you mean to bake and boil whatever you mean to boil. Put aside everything left over and keep it for the morning.” They set it aside until morning, just as Moses had ordered. It did not start to smell, and no maggots appeared in it. Moses said, “Today, eat this. Today is a Sabbath to the LORD; you will find none of it out in the field today. For six days you are to gather it. But the seventh day is a Sabbath, and on it there will be nothing to gather.” Even so, when the seventh day came, some of the people went out to gather it, and they found nothing.

Sabbath rest and the jar of manna

The LORD said to Moses, “How long will you people go on refusing to keep my commandments and my laws? Understand this: the LORD has given you the Sabbath. That is why on the sixth day he provides you with bread for two days. On the seventh day all of you are to stay where you are; no one is to leave home.” So on the seventh day the people rested. The people of Israel named it manna. It was like coriander seed, but white, and its taste was like honey wafers. Moses said, “Here is what the LORD has commanded: ‘Set aside a full 2 quarts of it to be kept for your descendants, generation after generation. Then they can look at the bread I gave you to eat in the wilderness after I brought you out of Egypt.’” Moses told Aaron, “Get a jar and put a full 2 quarts of manna into it. Then set it in the presence of the LORD, to be kept for all your generations to come.” Aaron set it in front of the testimony for safekeeping, as the LORD had told Moses to do. For forty years the Israelites ate manna, until they reached a land where people lived. They went on eating manna until they arrived at the edge of the land of Canaan. (An omer is about 2 quarts, one tenth of an ephah.)

fields.title: Exodus 17
fields.body_html:
Water from the rock

The whole community of the Israelites moved on from the wilderness of Sin, traveling in stages as the LORD commanded. They made camp at Rephidim, but there was no water there for the people to drink. The people turned on Moses in a quarrel. “Give us water to drink!” they demanded. Moses answered them, “Why pick a quarrel with me? Why put the LORD to the test?” But the people were thirsty there, and they grumbled against Moses. “Why did you ever bring us up out of Egypt?” they said. “Was it to make us die of thirst, with our children and our animals?” Moses cried out to the LORD, “What am I going to do with this people? A little more of this, and they will stone me!” The LORD told Moses, “Walk on ahead of the people, and bring some of Israel’s elders with you. Take along your staff, the one you struck the Nile with, hold it in your hand, and go. Look, I will be standing there before you, on the rock at Horeb. You are to strike the rock, and water will pour out of it, and the people will drink.” Moses did so, with the elders of Israel looking on. He named the place Massah, “testing,” and Meribah, “quarreling,” because there the Israelites quarreled, and there they put the LORD to the test by asking, “Is the LORD among us or not?”

Battle with Amalek

Then the Amalekites came and went to war with Israel at Rephidim. Moses said to Joshua, “Pick out men for us and go out to do battle with Amalek. Tomorrow I will take my stand on the hilltop, holding the staff of God in my hand.” Joshua did what Moses had told him and fought Amalek, while Moses, Aaron, and Hur climbed to the top of the hill. Whenever Moses held his hand high, Israel prevailed; and whenever he let it sink, Amalek prevailed. Moses’ hands grew heavy, so they got a stone and set it under him, and he sat on it. Aaron and Hur held up his hands, one of them on each side, and so his hands stayed firm until the sun set. So Joshua cut down Amalek and its fighting men with the edge of the sword.

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Record this in a scroll to be remembered, and say it over to Joshua: I will wipe out the memory of Amalek completely from under the heavens.” Then Moses built an altar there, and he gave it the name “The LORD Is My Banner.” He said, “A hand is lifted to the throne of the LORD! The LORD will fight Amalek generation after generation.”

fields.title: Exodus 18
fields.body_html:
Jethro’s visit and advice

Word reached Jethro, the priest of Midian and Moses’ father-in-law, of everything God had done for Moses and for Israel, his people: the LORD had brought Israel out of Egypt. Jethro, Moses’ father-in-law, had taken in Zipporah, Moses’ wife, after Moses had sent her back, along with her two sons. One of them was named Gershom, because Moses had said, “I have been an outsider in a foreign land.” The other was named Eliezer, because “The God of my father was my helper, and he rescued me from Pharaoh’s sword.” Moses’ father-in-law Jethro came out into the wilderness with Moses’ wife and sons, and found him camped at the mountain of God. He sent word to Moses, “I, your father-in-law Jethro, am on my way to you, along with your wife and her two sons.” Moses went out to meet his father-in-law. He bowed low and kissed him, and they asked after each other’s well-being. Then they went into the tent. Moses gave his father-in-law a full account of what the LORD had done to Pharaoh and to Egypt on Israel’s behalf. He told of every hardship that had come upon them on their journey, and of how the LORD had delivered them. Jethro was glad because of all the good the LORD had done for Israel when he rescued them from the power of Egypt. Jethro said, “Blessed be the LORD, who has delivered you from the grip of Egypt and of Pharaoh, and has freed this people from under Egypt’s hand. Now I know that the LORD is greater than all the gods, for he showed it in the very matter in which they acted proudly against Israel.” Then Moses’ father-in-law Jethro took a burnt offering and sacrifices and offered them to God. Aaron and every elder of Israel joined Moses’ father-in-law, and they ate a meal together before God. The following day Moses sat down to judge the people’s cases, and from morning to evening the people stood waiting before him. When Moses’ father-in-law saw all that he was doing for the people, he said, “What sort of thing is this you are doing with the people? Why do you sit here alone, while the whole crowd stands waiting on you from morning to evening?” Moses answered his father-in-law, “It is because the people come to me to inquire of God. Whenever they have a dispute, it comes to me, and I decide between the two sides. I also make God’s statutes and his laws known to them.” Moses’ father-in-law said to him, “This way of doing things is not good. You are sure to wear out, both you and the people who are with you. The load is too heavy for you; you cannot carry it by yourself. Now hear what I have to say. Let me counsel you, and may God be with you. Your part is to stand before God on the people’s behalf and to take their cases to God. Instruct them in the statutes and the laws, and show them the path they are to walk and the things they are to do. Then look over all the people and pick out able men, men who fear God, who can be relied on and who hate gain got by cheating. Put them in charge of the people as officers over thousands, over hundreds, over fifties and over tens. They will judge the people at all times. Every great matter they will bring to you, but every small matter they will decide themselves. So make your load lighter, and they will carry it with you. If you do this, and God gives you this command, you will be able to hold up, and all these people as well will go back to their homes in peace.” Moses took his father-in-law’s advice and did all he had proposed. From all Israel Moses picked able men and made them heads over the people: officers over thousands, over hundreds, over fifties and over tens. From then on they judged the people at all times. Any hard case they took to Moses, but every small matter they decided themselves. Then Moses saw his father-in-law off, and Jethro went back to his own land.

fields.title: Exodus 19
fields.body_html:
Israel at Mount Sinai

The Israelites arrived in the wilderness of Sinai on the day the third month began after their departure from the land of Egypt. They had moved on from Rephidim and come into the wilderness of Sinai, and there in the wilderness they set up camp. Israel camped there, facing the mountain. Moses went up to God, and the LORD called out to him from the mountain: “Say this to the house of Jacob, and declare it to the Israelites: ‘You saw with your own eyes what I did to the Egyptians, and how I lifted you up on eagles’ wings and brought you here to me. So now, if you truly listen to my voice and hold to my covenant, then of all the peoples you will be my own special treasure. The whole earth belongs to me, and you will be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation that belongs to me.’ These are the words you are to speak to the Israelites.” Moses came back and called the elders of the people together. He laid out for them all these words, just as the LORD had commanded him. The people answered as one: “We will do everything the LORD has spoken.” And Moses carried the people’s words back to the LORD. The LORD said to Moses, “Look, I am coming to you in a dark, heavy cloud, so that the people will hear when I speak with you and will trust you from now on.” Moses reported the people’s words to the LORD. The LORD told Moses, “Go to the people, and today and tomorrow consecrate them. They must wash their clothes and be prepared for the third day, for on the third day the LORD will descend upon Mount Sinai with all the people watching. Mark out a boundary for the people all the way around, and warn them, ‘Watch yourselves! Do not climb the mountain or even touch the edge of it. Anyone who touches the mountain is to be put to death. No one is to lay a hand on such a person; that one must be stoned or shot with arrows. Whether it is an animal or a human being, it must not live.’ When the ram’s horn sounds a long note, they may go up on the mountain.” Moses went down from the mountain to the people. He made them ready by consecrating them, and they washed their clothing. Moses told the people, “Be ready in three days’ time. Until then, no man is to have sexual relations with a woman.” When morning came on the third day, thunder crashed and lightning flashed. A heavy cloud lay on the mountain, and the ram’s horn blew very loudly. Everyone in the camp shook with fear. Moses brought the people out from the camp to meet God, and they took up their places below the mountain. All of Mount Sinai was smoking, since the LORD had come down upon it in fire. Its smoke went up like the smoke rising from a kiln, and the entire mountain shook with great force. The sound of the ram’s horn kept growing stronger and stronger. Moses would speak, and God would answer him with a voice like thunder. The LORD came down on Mount Sinai, onto the mountain’s summit, and called Moses up to the summit. So Moses went up. The LORD said to Moses, “Go down and give the people a strict warning, so that they do not push past the boundary toward the LORD to gaze, and many of them fall dead. And the priests who come near to the LORD must also consecrate themselves, so that the LORD does not burst out against them.” Moses answered the LORD, “There is no way the people can climb Mount Sinai. You gave us a warning: ‘Mark out a boundary around the mountain and treat it as holy.’” The LORD answered him, “Go back down, and then return, you and Aaron with you. As for the priests and the people, they are not to push through to come up to the LORD, or he will burst out against them.” Moses went down to the people and spoke to them.

fields.title: Exodus 20
fields.body_html:
The Ten Words

God spoke all these words, and said,

“I am the LORD your God. I brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house where you were slaves. You shall have no other gods besides me. You shall not make yourself a carved idol, nor a figure of anything in the heavens overhead, on the earth below, or in the waters beneath the earth. You shall neither bow to them nor serve them. For I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God. I bring the guilt of fathers upon their children, upon the third and the fourth generation of those who hate me, but to thousands who love me and keep my commandments I show faithful love.

You shall not use the name of the LORD your God for what is false or worthless, for the LORD will not let anyone go unpunished who uses his name that way.

Remember the Sabbath day and set it apart as holy. You have six days to labor and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath for the LORD your God. Do no work on it: not you, nor your son or daughter, nor your male or female servant, nor your livestock, nor the foreigner living among you in your towns. For the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea and everything in them, in six days, and on the seventh day he rested. For this reason the LORD blessed the Sabbath day and made it holy.

Honor your father and your mother. Then your days will be long in the land the LORD your God is going to give you.

You shall not murder. You shall not commit adultery. You shall not steal. You shall not give false evidence against your neighbor.

You shall not covet your neighbor’s household: you shall not set your heart on his wife, his male or female servant, his ox or his donkey, or anything else your neighbor has.”

The people keep their distance

All the people witnessed the thunder and the lightning, the blast of the ram’s horn and the smoking mountain. When they saw it, they trembled and stood back at a distance. They said to Moses, “You speak to us, and we will listen. But God must not speak to us, or we will die.” Moses answered the people, “Do not be afraid. God has come to test you, and to put the fear of him before your eyes, so that you will not sin.” So the people kept their distance, and Moses went up close to the thick darkness where God was.

Instructions about altars

The LORD said to Moses, “Say this to the Israelites: ‘You saw with your own eyes that I spoke with you from heaven. You shall not make gods to share my place; you shall not make yourselves gods of silver or gold. You are to make an altar of earth for me, and on it sacrifice your burnt offerings and your fellowship offerings, from your flocks and your herds. Wherever I cause my name to be remembered, I will come to you and bless you. If you make me an altar of stones, do not build it from cut stones. Once you swing your tool over it, you rob it of its holiness. Do not climb to my altar by steps, so that your nakedness is not exposed there.

fields.title: Exodus 21
fields.body_html:
Hebrew slaves

Here are the rules you are to lay before the people: When you acquire a Hebrew slave, he will serve six years; then in the seventh year he is to be released, free and owing nothing. If he arrived alone, he leaves alone. If he was married when he arrived, his wife leaves with him. If his master provides him with a wife and she bears him sons or daughters, the wife and her children remain the master’s, and he goes out on his own. But suppose the slave says plainly, ‘I love my master, my wife and my children. I will not leave as a free man.’ his master shall bring him to God. Then he shall stand him by the door or the doorpost and drive an awl through his ear, and the man will serve him as a slave for life.

If a man sells his daughter to be a maidservant, she does not leave at the end of six years as the male slaves do. Should her master, who had intended her for himself, find her displeasing, he must allow her to be redeemed. Since he has failed her, he may not sell her to people of another nation. If he intends her for his son, he must deal with her as he would with a daughter of his own. Should he take a second wife, the first is still to have her full share of food, clothing and marital rights. And if he fails her in these three things, she may leave free, with no price to pay.

Crimes deserving death

Whoever hits another person and kills them must be put to death. But if the killing was not planned, and God allowed it to happen, I will set aside a place for you where the killer can flee.

But if someone schemes against their neighbor and kills them by treachery, take the killer away even from my altar to be put to death.

Whoever strikes father or mother must be put to death. Whoever steals a person must be put to death, and it makes no difference whether the captive has been sold or is found still held.

Whoever curses father or mother must be put to death.

Injuries to people

Suppose two people fight, and one strikes the other with a rock or with a fist. The other does not die but is laid up in bed. If the injured person can get up and go about outdoors leaning on a staff, the attacker goes unpunished. But the attacker must make up for the work the injured one could not do, and pay until the healing is complete.

When an owner beats a male or female slave with a rod and the slave dies on the spot, the slave must be avenged. But if the slave lives on for a day or two, there is to be no vengeance, for the slave is the owner’s money.

When men are fighting and they hit a pregnant woman so that her children are born early, but no further harm follows, the guilty man must pay a fine. The woman’s husband sets the amount, and the payment is made as the judges determine. If harm does follow, the penalty is life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, gash for gash, welt for welt.

If an owner hits a slave, male or female, in the eye and blinds that eye, the slave goes free as payment for the lost eye.

The same holds for a tooth: a slave, man or woman, whose tooth the owner knocks out is to be freed for the tooth.

An ox that gores

When an ox kills a man or a woman with its horns, the animal is to be stoned and its meat left uneaten. Its owner, though, bears no guilt. It is different if the ox was known to gore before. If its owner had been told of the danger and still failed to keep it in, and it then kills a man or a woman, the ox must be stoned, and the owner too must die. But if the owner is offered a ransom instead, their life can be redeemed by paying the full amount that is set. If the ox gores a boy or a girl, the owner is dealt with by this same ruling. When the victim is a slave, man or woman, the ox’s owner pays about 12 ounces of silver to the slave’s master, and the ox is stoned.

Paying for a neighbor’s loss

Suppose someone opens up a pit or digs a new one and leaves it without a cover, and an ox or a donkey falls into it. The pit’s owner must make good the loss by paying the animal’s owner in silver, and may keep the dead animal.

If someone’s ox injures their neighbor’s ox and it dies, they are to sell the ox that is alive and share the price, and share the dead one too. But if people knew the ox had a habit of goring and its owner still left it loose, that owner must replace the dead ox with a live one, and the dead one becomes the owner’s.

fields.title: Exodus 22
fields.body_html:
Theft and damage to property

If someone steals an ox or a sheep and butchers it or sells it, the thief must replace the ox with five cattle and the sheep with four sheep. Suppose a thief is caught in the act of breaking in, and someone strikes him and he dies. Then there is no bloodguilt for his death. But if the sun is already up when it happens, the killing brings bloodguilt. The thief must repay in full; if he owns nothing, he is to be sold to make up for what he took. Should the animal he stole, whether an ox, a donkey or a sheep, still be alive and in his hands when it is found, he must repay double.

Suppose someone turns animals out to graze a field or a vineyard, and lets them loose so that they feed in another person’s field. Then the best that their own field and vineyard produce must be used to repay the loss.

Suppose a fire is lit, and it catches in the thorns and spreads, and stacked grain, grain still standing, or a whole field burns up. The person who lit the fire must pay in full for the loss.

Things left in a neighbor’s care

Suppose someone hands money or other things over to a neighbor to look after, and a thief takes them from that house. If the thief is found, he must repay twice the value. If the thief is not found, the owner of the house is to come before God and declare that he did not lay a hand on his neighbor’s goods. Whenever there is a charge of wrongdoing over an ox, a donkey, a sheep, a cloak or anything lost, and someone claims, ‘This is it,’ the two of them shall take their case to God. The one whom God condemns must repay their neighbor double.

Suppose someone entrusts a donkey, an ox, a sheep or any other animal to a neighbor’s care, and it dies, is hurt or is carried off when no one is there to see. Then the two of them shall settle it with an oath of the LORD: the one who kept the animal swears to having taken none of the neighbor’s property. The owner must accept the oath, and nothing has to be paid back. But if the animal was actually stolen from the one keeping it, that person must repay its owner. If beasts tore it to pieces, the keeper is to bring what is left as evidence and owes nothing for the animal that was torn.

Anyone who borrows a neighbor’s animal must make full repayment if it is hurt or dies while its owner is absent. But if the owner was present, there is no repayment. If the animal was rented, the owner’s loss is met by the rent.

A seduced virgin

If a man talks a virgin who is not betrothed into lying with him, he must pay the price paid for a bride and take her as his wife. Should her father flatly refuse to let him marry her, the man must still weigh out silver equal to the price paid for a virgin bride.

Death penalties and care for the weak

You shall not let a sorceress live.

Death is the penalty for anyone who lies with an animal.

Anyone who offers sacrifice to other gods, and not to the LORD alone, shall be devoted to destruction. Do no wrong to a foreigner living among you, and do not oppress anyone like that, because you yourselves lived as foreigners in the land of Egypt. You shall not afflict any widow or fatherless child. Should you afflict them, you can be sure that when they cry out to me, I will hear their cry, and my wrath will burn, and I will put you to death by the sword; your own wives will then be widows, and your children will have no fathers.

Lending to the poor

When you lend money to my people, to a poor person living near you, do not deal with that person as a creditor would, and do not make them pay interest. Should you hold your neighbor’s cloak as a pledge for a debt, you must hand it back to its owner before sunset, for it is the only covering they have, the cloak that wraps their body. In what will they lie down to sleep? When that neighbor cries out to me, I will hear, because I am gracious.

Firstfruits and firstborn

Do not speak contemptuously of God, and do not call down a curse on a leader of your people. Do not be slow to give from the abundance of your harvest or from what flows from your presses. Your firstborn sons you shall give to me. You are to do likewise with your oxen and your sheep: for seven days the firstborn remains with its mother, and on the eighth day you shall give it to me. You shall be holy people to me. Any meat torn by beasts out in the field is not for you to eat; it is to be thrown to the dogs.

fields.title: Exodus 23
fields.body_html:
Honest witness and fair justice

Do not pass along a false report. Do not join forces with a wicked person by serving as a witness whose words do violence.

Do not follow a crowd to do evil. And when you speak in a lawsuit, do not lean toward the many so as to bend justice. Do not give special treatment to a poor person in their lawsuit either.

When you find your enemy’s ox or donkey gone astray, you must lead it back to its owner.

Suppose the donkey of someone who hates you has sunk down under its burden. However much you may wish to leave it to them, you must work with them to set it free.

Justice, rest and the yearly feasts

Do not pervert the justice due to your poor when they bring a case. Stay far away from a false charge. Do not put to death one who is innocent and in the right, for I will not declare the wicked to be in the right. Take no bribe. A bribe blinds the clear-sighted and overturns the cause of those who are in the right. Do not oppress a foreigner living among you. You know from the inside what a foreigner’s life is like, since you yourselves were foreigners in the land of Egypt. For six years you are to sow your land and gather in its crops, but in the seventh you are to release it and let it lie, so that the needy among your people may eat from it, and the wild animals may eat what they leave. Treat your vineyard and your olive grove the same way. Work for six days, but on the seventh day stop, so that your ox and your donkey may rest, and the child of your female servant and the foreigner living among you may be refreshed. Be on guard in all that I have said to you. Do not make mention of the names of other gods; let no such name be heard from your mouth. Three times each year you shall keep a pilgrim feast in my honor. Observe the Feast of Unleavened Bread: you shall eat unleavened bread seven days, as I instructed you, at its fixed time in the month of Abib, the month when you left Egypt. And let no one come into my presence empty-handed. Keep also the Feast of Harvest, with the firstfruits of your labor, of what you sow in the field, and the Feast of Ingathering at the turn of the year, when you gather in from the field what your labor has produced. Three times a year every male among you is to present himself before the Lord GOD. Do not offer the blood of my sacrifice with anything leavened, and the fat from my feast must not be left over until morning. The best of your ground’s firstfruits you are to bring to the house of the LORD your God. You shall not boil a young goat in its mother’s milk.

An angel to lead the way

I am sending an angel to go before you. He will protect you on your journey and lead you to the place I have made ready. Take care in his presence and obey what he says. Do not defy him, because he will not pardon your wrongdoing; my name is in him. If you truly heed his voice and do everything I tell you, then I will be an enemy to your enemies and an adversary to those who stand against you. For my angel will go before you and bring you to the land of the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hivites and the Jebusites, and I will make an end of them. Do not bow down to their gods or serve them, and do not copy what they do. Instead, you are to pull those gods down completely and break their sacred pillars into pieces. Serve the LORD your God, and he will bless your bread and your water. I will take sickness away from among you. No woman in your land will lose her child before birth or be unable to bear children. I will let you live out the full number of your days. I will send terror of me ahead of you and throw every people you come against into panic. I will make all your enemies show you their backs. I will send the hornet in front of you, and it will chase the Hivites, the Canaanites and the Hittites out of your path. Yet I will not clear them away from before you within one year. If I did, the land would lie empty, and the wild animals would multiply and overrun you. I will drive them out from before you little by little, until you have grown many and can take the land as your own. I will fix your borders from the Red Sea to the Sea of the Philistines, and from the wilderness to the Euphrates River. I will hand over to you the people who live in the land, and you will drive them out before you. Make no covenant with them or with their gods. They must not live in your land, or they will lead you to sin against me. For you would come to serve their gods, and that would be a snare to you.”

fields.title: Exodus 24
fields.body_html:
The blood of the covenant

God also told Moses, “Come up to the LORD, you with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of Israel’s elders. You are to bow low in worship while still far off. Moses by himself is to approach the LORD. The rest are to stay back, and the people are not to climb the mountain with him.” Moses came and reported to the people all that the LORD had said, every word and every rule. The whole people answered together as one: “We will do every word the LORD has spoken.” Moses put all the words of the LORD in writing. He was up early the next morning to build an altar below the mountain, with twelve pillars, one for each tribe of Israel. He sent out young men of the Israelites. They presented burnt offerings and slaughtered bulls as fellowship offerings for the LORD. Moses kept half of the blood aside in bowls and dashed the rest against the altar. Then he took the scroll of the covenant and read it aloud for the people to hear. They answered, “Whatever the LORD has said, we will carry out. We will listen and obey.” Moses took the blood and dashed it over the people. “Look,” he said, “the blood of the covenant, which the LORD has made with you on the terms of all these words.” Moses then went up the mountain, with Aaron, Nadab and Abihu, and seventy of the elders of Israel. They saw the God of Israel. Beneath his feet there seemed to be a floor paved with sapphire, as pure and clear as the sky itself. Against the chief men of the Israelites he did not stretch out his hand. They gazed on God, and they ate and drank.

Moses on the mountain forty days

The LORD said to Moses, “Come up to me on the mountain and remain there. I will give you the tablets of stone, the law and commandment that I have written to teach the people.” Moses got up, along with Joshua who served him, and Moses climbed the mountain of God. To the elders he said, “Remain here for us until we return to you. Aaron and Hur will be with you; if anyone has a case to settle, they can go to those two.” Moses climbed the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain. The glory of the LORD came to dwell on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered the mountain six days. On the seventh day he called to Moses from inside the cloud. As the Israelites watched, the glory of the LORD appeared on the mountaintop like a fire that devours. Moses walked into the cloud and climbed the mountain, and there on the mountain he remained for forty days and forty nights.

fields.title: Exodus 25
fields.body_html:
Contributions for the sanctuary

The LORD said to Moses, “Speak to the Israelites and have them set aside a contribution for me. You are to receive my contribution from everyone whose heart moves them to give. This is the contribution you are to receive from them: gold, silver and bronze, blue, purple and scarlet yarn, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, fine leather, acacia wood, oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense, and onyx stones and other stones to be set in the ephod and the breastpiece. They are to make me a sanctuary, so that I may dwell among them. You are to make it in keeping with everything I show you, following the pattern of the tabernacle and the pattern of all its furnishings.

The ark

They are to make an ark of acacia wood, about 3 3/4 feet long, about 2 1/4 feet wide and about 2 1/4 feet high. Overlay it with pure gold on the inside and the outside, and put a gold molding around it on every side. Cast four rings of gold for it and fix them at its four feet, so that each side has two rings. You are also to make poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. Slide the poles through the rings on the sides of the ark, so that the ark can be carried by them. The poles are to be kept in the rings of the ark and never pulled out. Inside the ark you are to place the testimony that I will give you. Make a mercy seat of pure gold, about 3 3/4 feet long and about 2 1/4 feet wide. Make two cherubim of gold. Make them of hammered work, at the two ends of the mercy seat. Form one cherub at this end and another at that end. The cherubim are to be shaped out of the mercy seat itself, at its two ends. The cherubim are to spread their wings out above, sheltering the mercy seat with their wings. They are to face one another, with their faces turned toward the mercy seat. The mercy seat is to go on top of the ark, and inside the ark you are to put the testimony I will give you. I will meet with you there. I will speak with you from above the mercy seat, from the space between the two cherubim on the ark of the testimony, and give you every command meant for the Israelites.

The table

Make a table of acacia wood, about 3 feet long, about 1 1/2 feet wide and about 2 1/4 feet high. Overlay it with pure gold, and give it a gold molding all the way around. Give it a frame about 3 inches wide on every side, with a gold molding all around the frame. Make it four rings of gold and set them at the four corners, one by each of its four legs. Place the rings near the frame; they will hold the poles by which the table is carried. Make the poles from acacia wood and overlay them with gold. The table will be carried with them. Make its dishes, its pans, its jars and its bowls, which are used for pouring out drink offerings; make them of pure gold. On the table you are to set the bread of the Presence, to lie before me continually.

The lampstand

Make a lampstand of pure gold, hammered out. Its base and its shaft, its cups, its buds and its blossoms are to form one piece with it. Six branches are to come out from the sides of the lampstand: from one side three of its branches, and from the other side three. One branch is to have three cups shaped like almond blossoms, with a bud and a blossom, and the next branch three cups shaped like almond blossoms, with a bud and a blossom. It is to be the same for all six branches that come out of the lampstand. On the lampstand itself there are to be four cups shaped like almond blossoms, with its buds and blossoms. There is to be a bud under each pair of branches that come out of it: one bud beneath each of the three pairs, for the six branches that come out of the lampstand. Their buds and their branches are to be part of it, the whole of it a single hammered piece of pure gold. Make seven lamps for it. The lamps are to be mounted so that their light falls on the space before the lampstand. Its tongs and its fire pans are to be of pure gold. The lampstand and all these utensils are to be made from about 75 pounds of pure gold. Take care to make them by the pattern you are being shown on the mountain.

fields.title: Exodus 26
fields.body_html:
The tabernacle curtains

For the tabernacle you are to make ten curtains of fine twisted linen and of blue, purple and scarlet yarn. Have cherubim worked into them, the design of a skilled craftsman. Each curtain is to be about 42 feet long and about 6 feet wide; all the curtains are to have one measure. Five of the curtains are to be joined to one another, and the other five joined to one another as well. Put loops of blue yarn on the outer edge of the last curtain in the first set. Put them likewise on the edge of the outermost curtain of the second set. Put fifty loops on the one curtain and fifty on the end of the curtain in the second set, so that the loops line up with each other. Make fifty clasps of gold and join the two sets of curtains with them, one to the other. Then the tabernacle will be one whole.

The tent of goats’ hair

Then make eleven curtains of goats’ hair to be a tent over the tabernacle. Each curtain is to be about 45 feet long and about 6 feet wide; all eleven are to have one measure. Join five curtains together by themselves, and six by themselves. The sixth curtain is to be folded over double across the front of the tent. On the outer edge of the last curtain in the first set put fifty loops, and fifty more on the edge of the joining curtain in the second set. Make fifty clasps of bronze. Fit the clasps into the loops and join the tent together, so that it becomes one whole. Half of a curtain will be left over from the curtains of the tent. Let that surplus hang down over the rear of the tabernacle. In length the tent curtains will be longer by about 18 inches at each end. Let this surplus hang down over both sides of the tabernacle and cover it. Make a covering for the tent out of rams’ skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.

The frames

For the tabernacle make frames out of acacia wood, to stand upright. Make every frame about 15 feet high and about 2 1/4 feet wide. Every frame will have two tenons, joined one to the other. Do this for every frame of the tabernacle. The south side of the tabernacle is to have twenty frames. Under the twenty frames set forty bases of silver, two beneath every frame to receive its two tenons. For the other side of the tabernacle, the north side, make twenty frames with their forty silver bases, two under each frame. For the back of the tabernacle, the west end, make six frames. Two more frames are for the back corners of the tabernacle. They are to be double from the bottom and joined together at the top in a single ring. Both corner frames are to be made this way; they will form the two corners. The back wall will then have eight frames standing on sixteen silver bases, a pair beneath every frame. You are also to make crossbars from acacia wood, five of them for the frames along one side of the tabernacle, five for the frames of its other side, and five for the frames of the rear wall facing west. The middle crossbar, set halfway up the frames, is to reach all the way from one end to the other. Overlay the frames with gold, and make their rings of gold as holders for the crossbars; the crossbars too you are to overlay with gold. Erect the tabernacle following the design that was shown to you on the mountain.

The inner curtain and the screen

Make the inner curtain of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen. It is to be the work of a skilled craftsman, with cherubim worked into its design. Hang it from four pillars of acacia overlaid with gold. Their hooks are to be of gold, and they will stand on four bases of silver. Put the curtain in place beneath the clasps, and bring the ark of the testimony there, inside the curtain. For you it will mark the division between the holy place and the most holy place. Place the mercy seat on the ark of the testimony in the most holy place. Set the table outside the curtain, and the lampstand opposite the table, on the south side of the tabernacle. The table you are to put on the north side. Make a screen for the doorway of the tent from blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen, worked in colors by an embroiderer. Make five pillars of acacia wood for the screen and overlay them with gold; their hooks are to be gold. Cast five bases of bronze for them as well.

fields.title: Exodus 27
fields.body_html:
The altar

Make the altar out of acacia wood. It is to be square, about 7 1/2 feet on each side and about 4 1/2 feet high. Shape horns on its four corners, forming part of the altar itself, and overlay it all with bronze. Make its pots for clearing away the fat-soaked ashes, along with its shovels, basins, forks and firepans. All of its utensils are to be made of bronze. Make for it a grating of bronze, worked as a mesh, and attach four bronze rings to the mesh at its four corners. Place the grating beneath the ledge of the altar, down below, so that the mesh reaches to the middle of the altar. The altar is also to have poles: make them of acacia wood and overlay them with bronze. The poles are to be slid through the rings, so that they run along both sides of the altar whenever it is carried. The altar is to be a hollow box built of planks. Let them make it according to what you were shown on the mountain.

The courtyard

You are also to make the courtyard of the tabernacle. On the south side the courtyard is to have hangings of fine twisted linen, about 150 feet long on that one side. Its twenty pillars are to stand in twenty bronze bases, and the hooks and bands on the pillars are to be silver. The north side is to be the same: hangings about 150 feet long, with twenty pillars in twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands on the pillars. Across the width of the courtyard, on the west side, there are to be hangings about 75 feet long, with ten pillars and ten bases. The width of the courtyard on the east side, toward the sunrise, is also to be about 75 feet. On one side of the entrance there are to be hangings about 22 1/2 feet long, with three pillars and three bases. On the other side there are to be hangings about 22 1/2 feet long, with three pillars and three bases. The gateway of the courtyard is to have a screen about 30 feet wide, of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen, worked by an embroiderer, and hung on four pillars set in four bases. Every pillar around the courtyard is to be fitted with silver bands; their hooks are to be silver and their bases bronze. In all, the courtyard measures about 150 feet in length and about 75 feet across at each end. Its walls of fine twisted linen stand about 7 1/2 feet high, and the bases are bronze. All the tools used for every task in the tabernacle, and all its tent pegs and those of the courtyard, are to be made of bronze.

Oil for the lamp

You are to give the Israelites this command: they must bring you pure beaten olive oil for the light, to make a lamp burn continually. Aaron and his sons are to tend it in the tent of meeting, outside the curtain that screens the testimony, from evening to morning before the LORD. This is a statute for all time for the Israelites, generation after generation.

fields.title: Exodus 28
fields.body_html:
Garments for the priests

Now bring your brother Aaron near to you, and his sons with him, out from among the Israelites, to serve me as priests: Aaron and his sons Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar and Ithamar. You are to make holy garments for your brother Aaron, to clothe him with glory and beauty. Speak to all who are wise of heart, whom I have filled with a spirit of wisdom, and have them make Aaron’s garments to consecrate him, so that he may serve me as priest. The garments they are to make are these: a breastpiece, an ephod, a robe, a tunic of checkered weave, a turban and a sash. They will make holy garments for your brother Aaron and for his sons, for their service to me as priests. The workers are to take the gold, the blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and the fine linen.

The ephod

They are to make the ephod of gold, of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and of fine twisted linen, the work of a skilled designer. Two shoulder pieces are to be joined to its two ends, so that it is fastened together. The band woven to fasten it, which goes around it, must be made in the same way and form a single piece with it, of gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and fine twisted linen. Take two onyx stones, and on them engrave the names of the sons of Israel, six of their names on the first stone and the other six names on the second, in the order they were born. Cut the names of the sons of Israel into the two stones with the skill of a stone engraver cutting a seal. Enclose the stones in settings of gold filigree. Put the two stones on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel. Aaron will carry their names before the LORD on his two shoulders, for remembrance.

Make settings of gold filigree, and two chains of pure gold, braided the way cord is braided, and fasten these corded chains to the settings.

The breastpiece of judgment

Make a breastpiece of judgment, the work of a skilled designer. Make it in the same way as the ephod, of gold, of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and of fine twisted linen. It is to be square and folded double, about 9 inches long and about 9 inches wide. Fill it with mounted stones in four rows. In the first row are to be a carnelian, a topaz and a beryl; in the second row, a turquoise, a sapphire and an emerald; in the third row, a jacinth, an agate and an amethyst; and in the fourth row, a chrysolite, an onyx and a jasper. They are to be mounted in gold settings. The stones are to bear the names of the sons of Israel, twelve stones for their twelve names. Cut each one like a seal with its own name, for the twelve tribes. On the breastpiece make chains of pure gold, twisted like cords. Make two gold rings for the breastpiece, and put the two rings at two of its corners. Fasten the two gold cords to the two rings at the corners of the breastpiece. Fasten the other two ends of the two cords to the two settings, and so attach them to the shoulder pieces of the ephod at the front. Make two gold rings as well, and set them at the two lower ends of the breastpiece, on the edge that lies against the ephod, on the inner side. Make yet another two gold rings. Put them on the two shoulder pieces of the ephod toward the bottom of its front side, close to where it is joined, above the woven band of the ephod. Bind the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a blue cord, so that it stays on the woven band of the ephod and does not come away from it. So Aaron will carry the names of the sons of Israel on the breastpiece of judgment over his heart whenever he goes into the holy place, to keep them in remembrance before the LORD at all times. Put the Urim and the Thummim into the breastpiece of judgment, so that they are over Aaron’s heart when he goes in before the LORD. So Aaron will always carry, over his heart before the LORD, the judgment of the Israelites.

The robe

The robe that goes under the ephod is to be made wholly of blue. In the middle there is to be an opening for the head. Around the opening put a hem of woven work, like the neck of a coat of armor, so that it will not rip. Around its hem make pomegranates of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, all the way around, with gold bells between them all around, a gold bell and a pomegranate, a gold bell and a pomegranate, all around the hem of the robe. The robe is to be on Aaron when he ministers. As he enters the holy place to stand before the LORD, and as he leaves, its ringing will be heard, and so he will not die.

The gold plate and other garments

You are to make a plate of pure gold and cut on it, the way a seal is cut, the words ‘Holy to the LORD.’ Put it on a cord of blue and set it on the turban. It belongs on the turban’s front. Aaron is to wear it on his forehead. In this way he will carry the guilt of the holy things the Israelites consecrate, whatever holy gifts they bring. It will rest on his forehead at all times, so that they find acceptance before the LORD. Weave the tunic in a checkered weave from fine linen. The turban too is to be of fine linen. For the sash, make one worked in colors by an embroiderer. Aaron’s sons are also to have tunics; make sashes and caps for them as well, for glory and for beauty. Clothe your brother Aaron, and his sons with him, in these garments. Then anoint them, ordain them and consecrate them to serve me as priests. Make them linen undergarments to cover the nakedness of their bodies; they are to reach from the hips down to the thighs. These are to be on Aaron and his sons when they go into the tent of meeting, or when they come near the altar to serve in the holy place; then they will not bring guilt on themselves and die. It is a statute for all time for Aaron and for his descendants after him.

fields.title: Exodus 29
fields.body_html:
Ordaining the priests

Here is what you are to do to consecrate them as my priests: take one young bull and two rams with no defect, and unleavened bread, with unleavened loaves that have oil mixed in and thin unleavened wafers spread with oil. Use fine wheat flour for all of them. Place them all in a single basket and present them in it, along with the bull and the two rams. Next, have Aaron and his sons come forward to the doorway of the tent of meeting, and bathe them with water. Then take the priestly garments and put them on Aaron: the tunic, the robe that goes under the ephod, the ephod, and the breastpiece. Tie the ephod around him with its woven band. Place the turban on his head and fasten the holy crown to the turban. Then take the anointing oil and pour it over his head. In this way you will anoint him. Then bring his sons forward and dress them in tunics, and tie sashes around them, both Aaron and his sons, and fit caps on their heads. The priesthood will belong to them by a statute for all time. And you will ordain Aaron and his sons. Lead the bull to the front of the tent of meeting, where Aaron and his sons are to place their hands on its head. Slaughter the bull there before the LORD, at the doorway of the tent of meeting. With your finger, smear some of the bull’s blood on the horns of the altar, and pour out all the rest beside the altar’s base. Remove all the fat that covers the inner parts, the lobe that sits on the liver, and the two kidneys together with their fat, and turn them into smoke on the altar. As for the bull’s meat, its hide and its dung, burn them in a fire outside the camp. It is a sin offering. Next take the first ram. Aaron and his sons are to rest their hands on the ram’s head. Kill the ram, collect its blood, and throw it against the altar on all sides. Divide the ram into its pieces. Wash its insides and its legs, and set them beside its pieces and its head. Send up the whole ram in smoke from the altar as a burnt offering to the LORD. It is an offering by fire to the LORD, with an aroma that pleases him. Then take the other ram, and Aaron and his sons are to rest their hands on its head. Kill this ram and take some of its blood. Put the blood on Aaron’s right earlobe and on the right earlobes of his sons, on the thumbs of their right hands and the big toes of their right feet. Throw the rest of the blood against the altar all around. Then take a little of the blood on the altar and of the anointing oil, and spatter it on Aaron and his garments, and on his sons and their garments as well. In this way Aaron, his sons, and the garments they all wear will become holy. Take the fat of this ram, its fat tail, the fat that covers the inner parts, the lobe of the liver, the two kidneys and the fat around them, and the right thigh, because this ram is the ram of ordination, along with one round loaf of bread, one loaf made with oil, and one wafer from the basket of unleavened bread that stands before the LORD. Set all of it on the open hands of Aaron and his sons, and present it to the LORD with a waving motion as a wave offering. Afterward take these from their hands and send them up in smoke on the altar, on top of the burnt offering, as an aroma pleasing to the LORD. This is an offering by fire to the LORD. Then take the breast from the ram used to ordain Aaron, and present it to the LORD as a wave offering. That piece is to be your share. Consecrate the breast of the wave offering and the thigh of the contribution, the parts of the ram of ordination that were waved and lifted up, the share that belongs to Aaron and his sons. This will be the lasting share that Aaron and his sons receive from the Israelites. It is a contribution: whenever the Israelites sacrifice fellowship offerings, this part is their contribution to the LORD. The holy garments made for Aaron are to go to his sons after him. They will wear them when they are anointed and ordained. For seven days they are to be worn by whichever of his sons becomes priest in his place, when he enters the tent of meeting to serve in the holy place. As for the ram of ordination, boil its meat in a holy place. Aaron and his sons are to eat the ram’s meat, with the bread remaining in the basket, there at the doorway of the tent of meeting. The things that were used to make atonement for them, when they were ordained and made holy, are food for them to eat. An outsider must not eat any of it, since it is holy. Should any of the ordination meat or the bread remain until morning, you must burn whatever is left. No one may eat it; it is holy. Carry out for Aaron and his sons everything exactly as I have commanded you. Spend seven days ordaining them. Every day you are to offer a bull as a sin offering for atonement. You will cleanse the altar from sin as you make atonement for it, and you will anoint the altar so that it is consecrated. Seven days in a row you are to make atonement for the altar and consecrate it, and so it will become most holy. Anything that comes into contact with the altar will become holy.

The regular burnt offering

Here is what you will offer on the altar day by day, without fail: two lambs in their first year. One lamb you are to offer in the morning, and the second as evening falls. Along with the one lamb, there is to be about 2 quarts of fine flour mixed with about 1 quart of pure pressed olive oil, and for a drink offering, about 1 quart of wine. The second lamb you will offer as evening falls. Prepare with it a grain offering and a drink offering like those of the morning, an offering by fire to the LORD whose aroma pleases him. This is to be the regular burnt offering, generation after generation, at the doorway of the tent of meeting before the LORD. That is where I will meet with you, to speak to you. There I will meet with the Israelites, and my glory will make the tent holy. The tent of meeting and the altar I will make holy, and Aaron and his sons I will set apart as holy to serve me as priests. I will make my home among the Israelites, and I will be their God. Then they will know that I am the LORD their God. I brought them out of the land of Egypt for this purpose, to make my home among them. I am the LORD their God.

fields.title: Exodus 30
fields.body_html:
The altar of incense

You are to make an altar for burning incense, and you are to make it from acacia wood. Make it square, about 18 inches on each side and about 3 feet high, with its horns of one piece with it. Overlay it with pure gold: the top, the sides all the way around, and the horns. Then run a gold molding around it. Make two gold rings for it below the molding, on its two opposite sides, to hold the poles that it is carried with. Make the poles of acacia wood and overlay them with gold. Set it in front of the curtain that hangs before the ark of the testimony, in front of the mercy seat that covers the testimony, where I will meet with you. Each morning, as he sets the lamps in order, Aaron is to burn sweet-smelling incense on it. And when he lights the lamps at dusk he is to burn it again. This is to be the regular incense offered before the LORD, generation after generation. Never burn unauthorized incense on it. It is not for burnt offerings or grain offerings, and no drink offering may be poured out on it. Aaron is to make atonement on its horns one time each year, using blood from the sin offering of atonement. Once every year, generation after generation, atonement is to be made on it. It is most holy to the LORD.”

Atonement money

The LORD said to Moses, “Whenever you take a census of the Israelites and enroll them, every man is to give the LORD a ransom for his life at his enrollment. That way no plague will fall on them while the count is being made. Each one who crosses over to join those already counted is to give this: about 1/5 ounce of silver, weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary, which is twenty gerahs. This silver is a contribution to the LORD. All who cross over to the counted, from twenty years old and up, are to give this contribution to the LORD. When you bring the contribution to the LORD to make atonement for your lives, the rich are not to give more than the 1/5 ounce, nor the poor less. Collect the atonement money from the Israelites and put it toward the work of the tent of meeting. It will be a reminder before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites, making atonement for your lives.”

The bronze basin

The LORD said to Moses, “Make a basin of bronze on a bronze stand, to be used for washing. Set it between the tent of meeting and the altar and fill it with water. From it Aaron and his sons are to wash their hands and their feet. Each time they enter the tent of meeting, they must wash with water, so that they do not die. The same is true when they come near the altar to serve by burning an offering by fire to the LORD: they must wash their hands and feet, so that they do not die. This is a statute for all time, for Aaron and his descendants, generation after generation.”

The holy anointing oil

The LORD said to Moses, “Take for yourself the choicest spices: about 12 1/2 pounds of free-flowing myrrh; half that amount, about 6 1/4 pounds, of sweet-smelling cinnamon; about 6 1/4 pounds of fragrant cane; and about 12 1/2 pounds of cassia, all weighed by the shekel of the sanctuary; and about a gallon of olive oil. Out of these, prepare a holy oil for anointing, blended with a perfumer’s skill. It is to be the holy anointing oil. Use it to anoint the tent of meeting, the ark of the testimony, the table and all its utensils, the lampstand and its utensils, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand. In this way you are to consecrate them, and they will be most holy. Anything that touches them will become holy. Anoint Aaron and his sons, and consecrate them to serve me as priests. Tell the Israelites, ‘This is to be my holy anointing oil, generation after generation. It must not be poured on ordinary human flesh, and you must not make any oil like it by the same recipe. It is holy, and you are to treat it as holy. Whoever blends any like it, or puts any of it on someone who is not a priest, is to be cut off from their people.’”

The holy incense

The LORD said to Moses, “Take fragrant spices, stacte, onycha and galbanum, spices together with pure frankincense, an equal weight of each. Blend them into incense as a skilled perfumer would. It is to be seasoned with salt, pure and holy. Pound some of it into fine powder and set some before the testimony in the tent of meeting, where I will meet with you. You are to regard it as most holy. As for the incense you are to make, you must never make any by the same recipe for yourselves. You are to count it holy, belonging to the LORD. Whoever makes any like it for the pleasure of its scent is to be cut off from their people.”

fields.title: Exodus 31
fields.body_html:
Bezalel and Oholiab are chosen

The LORD said to Moses, “Take note: I have chosen Bezalel by name, the son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, and I have filled him with the Spirit of God, so that he has wisdom, understanding and knowledge in every kind of work, to think out artistic designs and to carry them out in gold, silver and bronze, to cut stones for mounting, to carve wood, and to do every kind of skilled work. I myself have also named Oholiab son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan, to be his partner. Into the hearts of all who are wise of heart I have put wisdom, so that they will make all that I have commanded you: the tent of meeting, the ark of the testimony with the mercy seat on top of it, and all the other furnishings of the tent; the table and its utensils, the lampstand of pure gold with all its utensils, the altar of incense, the altar of burnt offering with all its utensils, the basin with its stand, the finely woven garments, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons when they serve as priests, the oil for anointing, and the spiced incense for the sanctuary. In every detail they are to follow what I have commanded you.”

The Sabbath as a sign

The LORD also said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites: ‘Whatever else you do, keep my Sabbaths. The Sabbath is a sign between me and you for all your generations, so that you will know that I am the LORD, the one who sets you apart as holy. So you are to keep the Sabbath, for it is a holy day for you. If anyone profanes it, that person must be put to death. If anyone works on it, that person will be cut off from among their people. There are six days in which work may be done. The seventh day, though, is a Sabbath of full rest, set apart as holy to the LORD. Anyone who works on the Sabbath day must be put to death. The Israelites are to keep the Sabbath, holding to it generation after generation as a covenant for all time. It is a sign between me and the Israelites for all time, because in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, and on the seventh day he stopped working and was refreshed.’”

The two tablets of the testimony

When he had finished speaking with Moses on Mount Sinai, he gave him the two tablets of the testimony, tablets of stone inscribed by the finger of God.

fields.title: Exodus 32
fields.body_html:
The calf of gold

The people saw that Moses was a long time in coming down from the mountain. So they crowded around Aaron and said to him, “Get up and make us gods to lead the way for us. This Moses, the man who brought us up from the land of Egypt, we have no idea what has become of him.” Aaron told them, “Pull the gold rings out of the ears of your wives and your sons and daughters, and bring them here to me.” So all the people stripped the gold rings from their ears and brought them to Aaron. He took the gold from them, shaped it with an engraving tool, and made it into a calf of cast metal. Then they said, “Israel, these are your gods, who brought you up from the land of Egypt!” When Aaron saw this, he built an altar in front of the calf and made a proclamation: “Tomorrow we hold a feast to the LORD.” They were up early the next morning, offering burnt offerings and bringing fellowship offerings. Then the people sat down to a meal of food and drink, and rose up to revel.

Moses pleads for the people

Then the LORD said to Moses, “Go down at once! Your people, whom you brought up from the land of Egypt, have acted corruptly. So soon they have left the path I laid down for them! They have cast a metal calf for themselves, bowed down before it, offered sacrifices to it, and declared, ‘Israel, these are your gods, who brought you up from the land of Egypt!’” The LORD went on to say to Moses, “I have seen what this people is like. They are a stiff-necked people. So now let me alone, so that my wrath can burn hot against them and I can put an end to them. Then I will make you into a great nation.” But Moses sought the favor of the LORD his God. “LORD,” he said, “why should your anger blaze against your own people? You brought them out of the land of Egypt by great power and a strong hand. Why should the Egyptians say, ‘He brought them out to do them harm, to kill them among the mountains and put an end to them on the face of the earth’? Turn from your fierce anger, and relent from the harm you mean to bring on your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac and Israel, who served you. You swore to them by yourself and told them, ‘I will make your descendants as many as the stars in the sky. All this land I have spoken of I will give to your descendants, and it will be theirs for all time.’” And the LORD relented from the harm he had said he would do to his people.

Moses breaks the tablets

Then Moses turned and went down from the mountain, holding the two tablets of the testimony. These tablets were written on both sides, on the one face and on the other. God himself had made the tablets, and the writing cut into them was God’s own writing. When Joshua heard the noise of the people shouting, he said to Moses, “I hear the sound of war in the camp!” But Moses answered, “It is not the shout of men who have won, nor the wail of men who have lost. What I hear is the sound of singing.” As Moses came close to the camp, he saw the calf and the people dancing. He blazed with anger, flung down the tablets he was holding, and smashed them at the foot of the mountain. He took the calf they had made, burned it in the fire, and crushed it until it was fine dust. Then he scattered the dust over the water and made the Israelites drink it. Moses asked Aaron, “What had this people done to you, that you would bring so great a sin on them?” Aaron answered, “My lord, do not be so angry. You yourself know this people, how bent they are on doing wrong. They said to me, ‘Make us gods to lead the way for us. This Moses, the man who brought us up from the land of Egypt, we have no idea what has become of him.’ So I told them, ‘Anyone who has gold, pull it off.’ They handed it over to me, I tossed it into the fire, and out came this calf!” Moses saw that the people had broken loose. Aaron had let them run unchecked, so that they had become something for their enemies to sneer at. Moses took his stand at the gate of the camp and called out, “Who is on the LORD’s side? Come here to me!” And all the Levites rallied around him. He said to them, “This is what the LORD, the God of Israel, says: ‘Every man of you fasten his sword at his side. Pass through the camp from gate to gate and back again. Kill, every one of you, your brother, your friend and your neighbor.’” The Levites did as Moses ordered, and about 3,000 men of the people were killed that day. Moses said, “Today you have ordained yourselves for the LORD, for each of you took a stand against his own son and brother. And so this day a blessing has been given you.” The next day Moses told the people, “What you have done is a terrible sin. But I will go up again to the LORD. It may be that I can make atonement for your sin.” So Moses went back to the LORD and said, “Oh, hear me! This people has committed a terrible sin. They have made themselves gods out of gold. But now, if only you would forgive their sin! But if not, then blot me out of your book that you have written.” The LORD answered Moses, “It is the one who has sinned against me whom I will blot out of my book. Now go and lead the people to the place I told you of. My angel will go ahead of you. But when the day comes for me to call them to account, I will call them to account for their sin.” Then the LORD sent a plague on the people for making the calf, the calf that Aaron had made.

fields.title: Exodus 33
fields.body_html:
A grim message and the tent outside the camp

The LORD said to Moses, “Move on from here, you and the people whom you led up out of the land of Egypt. Head for the land I swore to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, the land of which I said, ‘To your offspring I will give it.’ I will send an angel ahead of you, and I will drive out the Canaanites, Amorites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. Go up to a land flowing with milk and honey. But I will not go up among you myself, since you are a stiff-necked people, and I might put an end to you on the road.” The people heard this grim message and grieved; not one of them put on their ornaments. The LORD said to Moses, “Tell the Israelites, ‘You are a stiff-necked people. Were I to go up among you even for a moment, I would put an end to you. So take off your ornaments now, and then I will settle what I am going to do about you.’” So from Mount Horeb onward the Israelites went without their ornaments. Moses made a practice of taking the tent and setting it up outside the camp, well away from it. He named it the tent of meeting. Whoever wanted to seek the LORD went out to the tent of meeting beyond the camp. When Moses set out for the tent, the whole people got to their feet. They stood, everyone at the door of their own tent, and followed Moses with their eyes until he went in. Each time Moses went into the tent, the pillar of cloud came down and took its place at the tent’s entrance, and the LORD spoke with Moses. Seeing the pillar of cloud at the tent’s entrance, the whole people would stand up and then bow low, everyone at the door of their own tent. The LORD would speak with Moses face to face, the way a person talks with a friend. Moses then went back to the camp; but Joshua son of Nun, the young man who served him, stayed in the tent and did not leave it.

Moses asks for God’s presence

Moses said to the LORD, “You tell me, ‘Bring this people up,’ yet you have not made known to me who is to go with me. You have also said, ‘I know you by name, and you have found favor in my sight.’ Now, if I really stand in your favor, please show me your ways. Then I will know you, and I will go on finding favor with you. And keep in mind that this nation belongs to you as your people.” The LORD answered, “My own presence will go along, and I will bring you to rest.” Moses said to him, “Unless your presence goes with us, do not make us leave this place. How else will anyone know that you look with favor on me and on your people? Is it not by your going with us? That is what sets me and your people apart from every other people on the face of the earth.”

Moses asks to see God’s glory

The LORD said to Moses, “This request too, the one you have just made, I will grant, because you have found favor in my sight and I know you by name.” Then Moses said, “Please, let me see your glory.” The LORD answered, “I will make all my goodness go past you, and I will announce the name ‘The LORD’ before you. I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious, and I will show compassion to whom I will show compassion.” He went on, “My face you cannot see. No human being can see me and stay alive.” The LORD said, “There is a place beside me. You are to stand there on the rock. While my glory is going by, I will tuck you into a cleft of the rock and shelter you with my hand until I have gone past. When I draw back my hand, you will see my back. But my face will not be seen.”

fields.title: Exodus 34
fields.body_html:
New tablets and the covenant renewed

The LORD said to Moses, “Cut two new tablets out of stone, like the first pair. On them I will write the same words that stood on the first tablets, which you smashed. Be prepared for the morning. When it comes, climb Mount Sinai and take your place before me on its summit. Nobody is to climb with you, and nobody else may be seen anywhere on the mountain. Keep even the flocks and herds from grazing near the front of that mountain.” So Moses cut two stone tablets like the first ones. Early next morning he went up Mount Sinai, as the LORD had commanded him, carrying the two stone tablets in his hand. The LORD came down in the cloud and took his place there beside Moses, and he announced his name, the LORD. The LORD passed in front of Moses and called out, “The LORD, the LORD, a God of tender compassion and grace, slow to grow angry, rich in faithful love and in truth, who keeps faithful love for thousands and forgives wrongdoing, rebellion and sin. Yet he will never acquit the guilty; he brings the wrongdoing of parents upon their children and grandchildren, to the third and the fourth generation.” Moses quickly sank down with his face to the ground in worship. He said, “Lord, if I really have found favor with you, then please, Lord, go in our midst. These are a stubborn people. Forgive our wrongdoing and our sin, and claim us as your own possession.” The LORD said, “Here and now I am making a covenant. In front of all your people I will work marvels such as have never been brought into being anywhere on earth or in any nation. All the people among whom you live will see what the LORD does, for what I am about to do with you will fill them with awe. Take care to keep what I am commanding you today. Watch: I am about to drive out ahead of you the Amorites, Canaanites, Hittites, Perizzites, Hivites and Jebusites. Watch yourself, so that you make no covenant with the people living in the land you are entering; otherwise it will become a trap set in your midst. Rather, you are to tear down their altars, shatter their standing stones, and chop down their Asherah poles. Bow down to no other god. The LORD is named Jealous; he is a jealous God. Do not make a covenant with the people who live in the land. For when they give themselves like prostitutes to their gods and offer sacrifices to them, someone will invite you, and you will eat from the sacrifice, and you will take some of their daughters as wives for your sons, and their daughters, prostituting themselves after their gods, will draw your sons after their gods in the same way. Do not make yourself gods cast from metal. Keep the Feast of Unleavened Bread: for seven days your bread is to be unleavened, as I commanded you, at its set time in the month of Abib, because it was in Abib that you left Egypt. Whatever first opens the womb is mine, including every male firstborn among your livestock, of cattle or of sheep and goats. Every firstborn donkey you are to redeem by giving a lamb in its place; if you will not redeem it, you must break its neck. And you are to redeem every firstborn son of yours. No one is to come before me with empty hands. For six days you may do your work, but the seventh day you are to keep as a day of rest. Rest even when the fields need plowing or the harvest is ready. Keep the Feast of Weeks when the first of the wheat harvest comes in, and the Feast of Ingathering as the year comes round. Three times a year every male among you is to appear before the Lord GOD, the God of Israel. I will dispossess nations to make room for you and push your borders outward. And while you are away three times a year, going up to appear before the LORD your God, no one will scheme to seize your land. When you slaughter a sacrifice for me, nothing leavened is to be offered with its blood. And nothing of the sacrifice of the Passover feast may be left over until morning. The choicest of the first produce from your land you are to bring into the house of the LORD your God. Never boil a young goat in the milk of its own mother.”

Moses’ face shines

The LORD told Moses, “Put these words in writing, for they are the terms on which I have made a covenant with you and with Israel.” Moses remained there with the LORD for forty days and forty nights; he ate no food and drank no water. And he wrote on the tablets the words of the covenant, the Ten Words. Moses came down from Mount Sinai holding the two tablets of the testimony. As he descended the mountain, he was unaware that the skin of his face shone with rays of light, because he had been speaking with God. When Aaron and all the Israelites looked at Moses, there was the skin of his face, shining, and they feared to approach him. Moses called them over, so Aaron came back to him, together with all the leaders of the community, and Moses spoke with them. After that all the Israelites came near, and Moses passed on to them as commands everything the LORD had told him on Mount Sinai. Once Moses was done speaking with them, he covered his face with a veil. Each time Moses went into the presence of the LORD to talk with him, he kept the veil off until he came out again. Then he would come out and tell the Israelites what he had been commanded to say. The Israelites saw the light shining from the skin of Moses’ face, and Moses would cover his face with the veil again until he went in to speak with him.

fields.title: Exodus 35
fields.body_html:
Sabbath rest

Moses gathered the whole community of the Israelites and said to them, “These are the things the LORD has commanded you to do: There are six days in which work may be done, but the seventh day is to be holy for you, a Sabbath of full rest to the LORD. Anyone who works on it must be put to death. On the Sabbath day no fire is to be lit anywhere you live.”

Gifts for the tent of meeting

Then Moses told the whole community of the Israelites, “This is what the LORD has commanded: Set aside among yourselves a contribution for the LORD.
