Everyone whose heart moves them to give is to bring it as the LORD’s contribution: gold, silver and bronze; blue, purple and scarlet yarn, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red, fine leather, acacia wood, oil for the lamps, spices for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense, and onyx stones and other stones to be set in the ephod and the breastpiece. Every one of you who is wise of heart is to come and make all that the LORD has commanded: the tabernacle with its tent and its covering, its clasps, frames, crossbars, pillars and bases; the ark and its poles, the mercy seat, and the curtain that screens it off; the table with its poles and all its utensils, and the bread of the Presence; the lampstand for the light with its utensils and its lamps, and the oil for the light; the altar of incense with its poles, the anointing oil and the fragrant incense, and the screen for the doorway at the entrance to the tabernacle; the altar of burnt offering with its bronze grating, its poles and all its utensils; the basin with its stand; the hangings of the courtyard with its pillars and bases, and the screen for the gateway of the courtyard; the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the courtyard, with their cords; the finely woven garments for service in the sanctuary, both the holy garments for Aaron the priest and the garments for his sons when they serve as priests.” Then the whole community of the Israelites went out from Moses. Then each one whose heart stirred them, and each one whose spirit moved them to give, came with the LORD’s contribution, to be used in building the tent of meeting, in all the service there, and in making the holy garments. They came, the men along with the women, all who had willing hearts, and they brought brooches, earrings, signet rings and pendants, every kind of gold object. Everyone who dedicated gold to the LORD as a wave offering brought it. And whatever blue, purple and scarlet yarn, fine linen, goats’ hair, rams’ skins dyed red and fine leather people had, they brought. Those who set aside silver or bronze brought it as a contribution for the LORD. People who had acacia wood that would serve for any of the work brought that as well. All the women who were wise of heart spun by hand, and they brought in the blue, purple and scarlet yarn and the fine linen they had spun. All the women whose hearts stirred them to use their skill spun the goats’ hair. The leaders brought the onyx stones and the other stones to be set in the ephod and the breastpiece, and the spices and the oil for the lamps, for the anointing oil and for the fragrant incense. The Israelites, every man and every woman whose heart moved them to give toward any of the work the LORD had commanded through Moses, brought it to the LORD as a freewill offering.

Skilled workers for the sanctuary

Then Moses said to the Israelites, “Take note: the LORD has chosen Bezalel by name, the son of Uri, son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, and he has filled him with the Spirit of God, so that he has wisdom, understanding and knowledge in every kind of work, to think out artistic designs and to carry them out in gold, silver and bronze, to cut stones for mounting, to carve wood, and to do every kind of artistic work. He has also given the ability to teach to Bezalel and to Oholiab son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan. He has filled them with wisdom of heart to carry out every task of the engraver, of the designer, of the embroiderer in blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen, and of the weaver. They can do every kind of work and think out artistic designs.

fields.title: Exodus 36
fields.body_html:
The people give more than enough

Bezalel, Oholiab and every skilled person whom the LORD has gifted with skill and understanding, so that they know how to do every task in the service of the sanctuary, will carry out the work exactly as the LORD has commanded.” Moses called for Bezalel and Oholiab, along with all whom the LORD had made skillful, everyone whose heart stirred them to come forward and do the work. Moses handed over to them all the contributions that the Israelites had brought for the work of the sanctuary service, so that they could carry it out. Still the people kept bringing him freewill offerings every morning. So all the skilled workers who were carrying out the work of the sanctuary came, each one leaving the task in hand, and told Moses, “The people keep bringing more than enough for the task the LORD has commanded us to carry out.” Moses gave a command, and it was announced throughout the camp: “Men and women alike must stop preparing gifts for the sanctuary.” So the people were held back from bringing any more. The materials they had were enough for all the work, and there was some to spare.

Making the tabernacle curtains

All the skilled craftsmen among the workers made the tabernacle from ten curtains of fine twisted linen and of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, with cherubim worked into them, the design of a skilled craftsman. Each curtain was about 42 feet long and about 6 feet wide; all the curtains had one measure. They joined five of the curtains to one another, and the other five they joined to one another as well. They put loops of blue yarn on the outer edge of the last curtain in the first set, and likewise on the edge of the outermost curtain of the second set. They put fifty loops on the one curtain and fifty on the end of the curtain in the second set, so that the loops lined up with each other. They made fifty clasps of gold and joined the two sets of curtains with them, one to the other. So the tabernacle became one whole.

Making the tent of goats’ hair

Then they made eleven curtains of goats’ hair to be a tent over the tabernacle. Each curtain was about 45 feet long and about 6 feet wide; all eleven had one measure. They joined five curtains together by themselves, and six by themselves. On the outer edge of the last curtain in the first set they put fifty loops, and fifty more on the edge of the joining curtain in the second set. They made fifty clasps of bronze to join the tent together so that it became one whole. They made a covering for the tent out of rams’ skins dyed red, and over that a covering of fine leather.

Making the frames and the inner curtain

They made frames of acacia wood for the tabernacle, to stand upright. Every frame was about 15 feet high and about 2 1/4 feet wide. Every frame had two tenons, joined one to the other. They did this for every frame of the tabernacle. For the south side of the tabernacle they made twenty frames. Under the twenty frames they made forty bases of silver, two beneath every frame to receive its two tenons. For the other side of the tabernacle, the north side, they made twenty frames with their forty silver bases, two under each frame. For the back of the tabernacle, the west end, they made six frames. They made two more frames for the back corners of the tabernacle. They were double from the bottom and joined together at the top in a single ring. They made both corner frames this way, for the two corners. So the back wall had eight frames standing on sixteen silver bases, a pair beneath every frame. They also made crossbars from acacia wood, five of them for the frames along one side of the tabernacle, five for the frames of its other side, and five for the frames of the rear wall facing west. They made the middle crossbar to run halfway up the frames, reaching from one end to the other. They overlaid the frames with gold and made their rings of gold as holders for the crossbars; the crossbars too they overlaid with gold. They made the inner curtain of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen, with cherubim worked into its design by a skilled craftsman. For it they made four pillars of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. Their hooks were gold, and they cast four bases of silver for them. They made a screen for the doorway of the tent from blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen, worked in colors by an embroiderer. They also made its five pillars with their hooks. They overlaid the tops of the pillars and their bands with gold, and the five bases were bronze.

fields.title: Exodus 37
fields.body_html:
Making the ark

Bezalel made the ark of acacia wood, about 3 3/4 feet long, about 2 1/4 feet wide and about 2 1/4 feet high. He overlaid it with pure gold on the inside and the outside, and put a gold molding around it on every side. He cast four rings of gold for it, set at its four feet, so that each side had two rings. He made carrying poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. He slid the poles through the rings on the sides of the ark, so that the ark could be carried. He made a mercy seat of pure gold, about 3 3/4 feet long and about 2 1/4 feet wide. He made two cherubim of gold, hammered out, for the two ends of the mercy seat. There was one cherub at this end and another at that end. He shaped the cherubim out of the mercy seat itself, at its two ends. The cherubim spread their wings out above, sheltering the mercy seat with their wings. They faced one another, with their faces turned toward the mercy seat.

Making the table

He made the table of acacia wood, about 3 feet long, about 1 1/2 feet wide and about 2 1/4 feet high. He overlaid it with pure gold and gave it a gold molding all the way around. He gave it a frame about 3 inches wide on every side, with a gold molding all around the frame. He cast four rings of gold for it and set them at the four corners, one by each of its four legs. The rings were near the frame, to hold the poles by which the table was carried. He made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with gold, for carrying the table. He made the utensils for the table out of pure gold: its dishes, its pans, its bowls, and the jars used for pouring out drink offerings.

Making the lampstand

He made the lampstand of pure gold, hammered out. Its base and its shaft, its cups, its buds and its blossoms formed one piece with it. Six branches came out from the sides of the lampstand: from one side three of its branches, and from the other side three. One branch had three cups shaped like almond blossoms, with a bud and a blossom, and the next branch three cups shaped like almond blossoms, with a bud and a blossom. It was the same for all six branches that came out of the lampstand. Four cups shaped like almond blossoms, with their buds and blossoms, were on the lampstand itself. There was a bud under each pair of branches that came out of it: one bud beneath each of the three pairs, for the six branches that came out of it. Their buds and their branches were part of it, the whole of it a single hammered piece of pure gold. He made seven lamps for it, along with its tongs and its fire pans, all of pure gold. From about 75 pounds of pure gold he made the lampstand and all its utensils.

Making the altar of incense

He made the altar of incense from acacia wood, square in shape, about 18 inches on each side and about 3 feet high; its horns were part of the altar itself. He overlaid it with pure gold: the top, the sides all the way around, and the horns. And he ran a gold molding around it. Below the molding he made two gold rings for it, on its two opposite sides, as holders for the carrying poles. He made its poles from acacia wood and overlaid them with gold. He also made the holy anointing oil and the pure incense of fragrant spices, prepared with a perfumer’s skill.

fields.title: Exodus 38
fields.body_html:
Making the altar of burnt offering

He made the altar of burnt offering out of acacia wood. It was square, about 7 1/2 feet on each side and about 4 1/2 feet high. He shaped horns on its four corners, forming part of the altar itself, and overlaid it with bronze. He made all the utensils for the altar: the pots, shovels, basins, forks and firepans. He made all its utensils of bronze. He made for the altar a grating of bronze, worked as a mesh, and set it under its ledge, reaching from below up to the middle of the altar. He cast four rings for the four corners of the bronze grating, to hold the poles. He made the poles of acacia wood and overlaid them with bronze. He slid the poles through the rings on the sides of the altar for carrying it. He built the altar as a hollow box of planks.

He made the basin and its stand of bronze. The bronze came from the mirrors of the women who served at the entrance of the tent of meeting.

Making the courtyard

He made the courtyard. On the south side the hangings of the courtyard were of fine twisted linen, about 150 feet long. There were twenty pillars in twenty bronze bases, with hooks and bands of silver on the pillars. The north side was also about 150 feet long, with twenty pillars in twenty bronze bases, and silver hooks and bands on the pillars. On the west side there were hangings about 75 feet long, with ten pillars and ten bases, and silver hooks and bands on the pillars. The east side, facing the sunrise, was also about 75 feet wide. On one side of the entrance there were hangings about 22 1/2 feet long, with three pillars and three bases. The other side was the same, so that there were hangings of about 22 1/2 feet on each side of the courtyard gate, with three pillars and three bases. All the hangings around the courtyard were of fine twisted linen. The bases of the pillars were bronze, and the hooks and bands on the pillars were silver. Their tops were overlaid with silver, and every pillar of the courtyard was fitted with silver bands. The screen for the courtyard gate was worked in colors by an embroiderer, of blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine twisted linen. It was about 30 feet long and about 7 1/2 feet high, matching the hangings of the courtyard. It hung on four pillars set in four bronze bases. Their hooks were silver, and so were the overlay on their tops and their bands. All the tent pegs for the tabernacle and for the courtyard around it were bronze.

Metals used for the tabernacle

This is the record of the tabernacle, the tabernacle of the testimony, as it was counted at Moses’ command. The counting was the work of the Levites, led by Ithamar son of Aaron the priest. It was Bezalel son of Uri, son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah, who made all that the LORD had commanded Moses. With him was Oholiab son of Ahisamach, of the tribe of Dan, an engraver and designer, who also worked in colors with blue, purple and scarlet yarn and fine linen.

All the gold used for the work, for all the work on the sanctuary, was gold given as an offering. It came to about 2,200 pounds, by the shekel of the sanctuary. The silver given by those of the community who were enrolled weighed about 7,500 pounds, by the shekel of the sanctuary. That was about 1/5 ounce a head, half a shekel by the shekel of the sanctuary, from every man twenty years old and up who crossed over to join those enrolled, 603,550 men in all. The 7,500 pounds or so of silver went to cast the bases of the sanctuary and the bases of the curtain. There were 100 bases, and each took about 75 pounds. From the remaining 45 pounds or so he made hooks for the pillars, overlaid their tops and fitted them with bands. The bronze given as an offering came to about 5,300 pounds. Out of it he made the bases for the entrance of the tent of meeting, the bronze altar together with the bronze grating that belonged to it, all the utensils of the altar, the bases all around the courtyard, the bases of the courtyard gate, and all the tent pegs of the tabernacle and of the courtyard on every side.

fields.title: Exodus 39
fields.body_html:
Making the priestly garments

Out of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, finely woven garments were made for service in the holy place. Aaron’s holy garments were made as well, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

Bezalel made the ephod from gold, blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and fine twisted linen. Gold was beaten into thin plates and cut into threads, which were worked in among the blue yarn, the purple, the scarlet and the fine linen with a designer’s skill. They made shoulder pieces for the ephod to join it together; it was fastened at its two ends. The woven band that went around it to fasten it was made the same way, in one piece with the ephod, of gold, of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and of fine twisted linen, as the LORD had commanded Moses. They prepared the onyx stones, mounted them in settings of gold filigree, and engraved them, as a seal is engraved, with the names of the sons of Israel. Bezalel set them on the shoulder pieces of the ephod as stones of remembrance for the sons of Israel, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

Making the breastpiece

He made the breastpiece with a designer’s skill, worked like the ephod, of gold, of blue, purple and scarlet yarn, and of fine twisted linen. It was square. They made the breastpiece folded double, about 9 inches long and about 9 inches wide when doubled. They set four rows of stones on it. In the first row were a carnelian, a topaz and a beryl; in the second row, a turquoise, a sapphire and an emerald; in the third row, a jacinth, an agate and an amethyst; and in the fourth row, a chrysolite, an onyx and a jasper. They were mounted in gold filigree settings. The stones bore the names of the sons of Israel, twelve of them to match their names. Each was engraved like a seal with its own name, for the twelve tribes. On the breastpiece they made chains of pure gold, twisted like cords. They also made a pair of gold filigree settings and a pair of gold rings; the rings they put on two corners of the breastpiece. They tied the two gold cords into the two rings at the corners of the breastpiece. The remaining ends of the cords went to the two settings, which they fixed to the front of the ephod on its shoulder pieces. They made two gold rings and set them at the two lower ends of the breastpiece, on its inner edge, the edge facing the ephod. They made another two gold rings and put them on the two shoulder pieces of the ephod, low on its front, near where it is joined, above the woven band of the ephod. They bound the breastpiece by its rings to the rings of the ephod with a blue cord, so that it lay on the woven band of the ephod and did not come away from it, as the LORD had commanded Moses. Bezalel made the robe that goes under the ephod, a weaver’s work, all of blue. The opening of the robe was in the middle, like the neck of a coat of armor, with a hem all around it so that it would not rip. On the hem of the robe they made pomegranates of twisted blue, purple and scarlet yarn. They made bells of pure gold too, and put the bells between the pomegranates all the way around the hem of the robe. Bell and pomegranate, bell and pomegranate, they went all around the hem of the robe, which was worn for ministering, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

They made tunics of fine linen, a weaver’s work, for Aaron and his sons, the turban of fine linen, the decorative caps of fine linen, and the linen undergarments of fine twisted linen, and the sash of fine twisted linen with blue, purple and scarlet yarn, worked in colors by an embroiderer, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

From pure gold they made the plate that is the holy crown, and they engraved it, as a seal is engraved, with the words “Holy to the LORD.” To it they attached a cord of blue so that it could be fixed high on the turban, as the LORD had commanded Moses.

The work is finished

In this way the whole work of the tabernacle, the tent of meeting, was finished. The Israelites carried out everything the LORD had commanded Moses; they did it all.

Then they brought the tabernacle to Moses: the tent and everything that belonged to it, its clasps, frames, crossbars, pillars and bases, the covering of rams’ skins dyed red and the covering of fine leather, and the curtain that screened the ark, the ark of the testimony with its poles, and the mercy seat, the table with all its utensils and the bread of the Presence, the lampstand of pure gold with its lamps set in a row, all its utensils, and the oil for the light, the gold altar, the oil for anointing, the spiced incense, and the screen for the doorway of the tent, the bronze altar with the bronze grating that belonged to it, its poles and all its utensils, and the basin with its stand, the hangings of the courtyard with its pillars and bases, the screen for the courtyard gate, its cords and tent pegs, and all the utensils for the work of the tabernacle, the tent of meeting, and the finely woven garments for serving in the holy place: the holy garments for Aaron the priest and his sons’ garments for their service as priests. In every detail the Israelites had done the whole work as the LORD had commanded Moses. Moses looked at all the work, and there it was, done in every point as the LORD had commanded. And Moses blessed them.

fields.title: Exodus 40
fields.body_html:
Instructions to set up the tabernacle

The LORD said to Moses, “On the first day of the first month, set up the tabernacle, the tent of meeting. Place the ark of the testimony in it, and screen the ark off with the curtain. Bring in the table and set out in order what belongs on it. Bring in the lampstand and mount its lamps. Place the gold altar for incense in front of the ark of the testimony, and hang the screen at the entrance to the tabernacle. Set the altar of burnt offering in front of the entrance to the tabernacle, the tent of meeting. Place the basin between the tent of meeting and the altar, and put water in it. Set up the courtyard all around it, and hang the screen at the gate of the courtyard. Then take the anointing oil and anoint the tabernacle and everything in it. Consecrate it and all its furnishings, and it will be holy. Anoint the altar of burnt offering and all its utensils. Consecrate the altar, and it will be most holy. Anoint the basin with its stand, and consecrate it. Bring Aaron and his sons to the entrance of the tent of meeting and wash them with water. Dress Aaron in the holy garments, anoint him and consecrate him, so that he may serve me as priest. Then bring his sons forward and put tunics on them. Anoint them as you anointed their father, so that they too may serve me as priests. Their anointing will give them a priesthood that lasts for all time, through every generation.” Moses carried out all that the LORD had commanded him. That is just what he did.

Moses sets up the tabernacle

In the second year, on the first day of the first month, the tabernacle was put up. Moses set up the tabernacle. He laid its bases, put its frames in place, fitted its crossbars and raised its pillars. He spread the tent over the tabernacle and laid the covering of the tent on top of it, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

He took the testimony and placed it in the ark, fitted the poles to the ark, and set the mercy seat on top of the ark. He brought the ark into the tabernacle and hung the curtain that serves as a screen, shutting off the ark of the testimony from view, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

He placed the table in the tent of meeting on the north side of the tabernacle, outside the curtain. He set out the bread on it in rows before the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

He placed the lampstand in the tent of meeting across from the table, on the south side of the tabernacle. He set up the lamps before the LORD, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

He placed the gold altar in the tent of meeting, in front of the curtain, and burned sweet-smelling incense on it, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

He hung the screen at the entrance to the tabernacle. He set the altar of burnt offering at the entrance to the tabernacle, the tent of meeting, and offered on it the burnt offering and the grain offering, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

Between the tent of meeting and the altar he placed the basin, and he filled it with water for washing. Moses, Aaron and Aaron’s sons would wash their hands and feet with water from it. Each time they went into the tent of meeting or came near the altar, they washed, just as the LORD had commanded Moses.

He put up the courtyard all around the tabernacle and the altar, and hung the screen for the courtyard gate. So Moses completed the work.

The cloud and the glory

Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the tabernacle was filled with the glory of the LORD. Moses was unable to go into the tent of meeting, since the cloud had come to rest on it and the tabernacle was full of the glory of the LORD. Whenever the cloud rose from over the tabernacle, the Israelites broke camp and moved on, at every stage of their journeys. If the cloud stayed where it was, they stayed too, until the day it rose. By day the cloud of the LORD rested over the tabernacle, and by night fire glowed within it. The whole house of Israel could see it, at every stage of their travels.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
By day the cloud of the LORD rested over the tabernacle, and by night fire glowed within it. The whole house of Israel could see it, at every stage of their travels.

— Exodus 40:38

Exodus does not end in the promised land. It ends in the wilderness, at the foot of a mountain, with a tent and a cloud. The slaves are free, the covenant is made, and God has come to live among them. But the journey has hardly begun, and the last chapter says so: the cloud will rise, and they will move on, “at every stage of their journeys.”

The question the book leaves with you

The deepest question in Exodus is not whether God can defeat Pharaoh. It is whether a holy God can live among the people he has rescued. The book’s answer is yes, but at a cost, and not yet completely. At the burning bush Moses had to take off his sandals. At Sinai the people stood back at a distance and begged not to hear God’s voice. After the golden calf God said he would not go up among them, “since you are a stiff-necked people”, and only Moses’ prayer changed that. And in the very last scene, when the glory fills the tabernacle, even Moses cannot go in.

So the book leaves its readers with Moses’ own question: will God go with us? “Unless your presence goes with us, do not make us leave this place.” And with a second question hidden inside the first: how can sinful people come near to him and live? The next book, Leviticus, opens at the door of that tent, “From the tent of meeting the LORD called to Moses”, and spends itself on the answer.

Where the story goes next

The exodus became the pattern for every later rescue in the Bible. The psalmists sing it, the prophets promise a new one, and when the first Christians wanted to say what Jesus had done, they reached for its words. John writes that “The Word became flesh and made his home among us. We have seen his glory”, using a word that recalls the tent where the glory dwelt. Luke says that on the mountain of the transfiguration Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus of “the exodus he was about to complete in Jerusalem.” Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb, and says of the rock in the wilderness, “and that rock was Christ.”

And the story ends where Exodus was always heading. In the last book of the Bible, those who have overcome stand beside a sea of glass and “sing the song of Moses, the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb”, and a voice from the throne announces what the tabernacle only foreshadowed:

“See, God’s dwelling is with human beings! He will make his home with them, and they will be his peoples; God himself will be with them.”

— Revelation 21:3

Where to go from here

Exodus has fed Christian preaching, prayer and teaching for as long as there has been a church. A few places to begin in this library:

  • On the whole book. Hannah Whitall Smith’s Old Testament Types and Teachings, whose chapter “Exodus: God’s Redemption” reads the book as the story of God’s way of redeeming his people, set beside Romans 3.
  • On the God who hears the oppressed (Exodus 3). Absalom Jones’s A Thanksgiving Sermon on the Abolition of the African Slave Trade, preached in Philadelphia on 1 January 1808 on Exodus 3:7–8; and Gareth Evans’s Four Reasons We Need Revival in North America, which begins with Moses at the burning bush (Exodus 3:1–6).
  • On the rock in the wilderness (Exodus 17). Christmas Evans’s The Smitten Rock, on 1 Corinthians 10:4, which follows the rock struck at Horeb to Calvary.
  • On the covenant and the Ten Commandments (Exodus 19–20). Andrew Murray’s The Two Covenants, whose chapter “The First Covenant” begins from Exodus 19:5; Thomas Watson’s The Ten Commandments; Martin Luther’s Large Catechism, which begins with the commandments one by one; and Book 2, Chapter 8 of John Calvin’s Institutes of the Christian Religion, “Exposition of the Moral Law”.
  • On the tabernacle (Exodus 25–40). Gareth Evans’s Burdens and Gifts (Exodus 25:40); and Horatius Bonar’s The Rent Veil, which moves from the veil of the tabernacle to the veil torn at the cross.
  • On Moses the intercessor (Exodus 32–34). E. M. Bounds’s Prayer and Praying Men, with its chapter “Moses, the Mighty Intercessor”; Andrew Murray’s The Inner Chamber, with “Moses, the Man of Prayer”; Gareth Evans’s Broken Before the Throne (Exodus 33:18–23); and A. W. Tozer’s The Hidden Life of Faith, on the cleft of the rock (Exodus 33:22).
  • On the faith of Moses. J. C. Ryle’s Holiness, with its chapter “Moses — An Example”, on Hebrews 11:24–26.

You can also go the other way, from the text to the classics. Every reference to Exodus in this library can be tapped to read the verse, and the Scripture pages gather, chapter by chapter, what the great writers of the church have said about each passage of this book.

And then read on, because the cloud is about to lift. The people who were carried out of Egypt on eagles’ wings still have a wilderness to cross, and they carry with them the promise Moses was given when he asked whether God would come:

The LORD answered, “My own presence will go along, and I will bring you to rest.”

— Exodus 33:14
